docs.text: The shape carries the meaning, not the colour. VERIFIED (solid outline) means we read the original source or measured it ourselves. LIKELY (dashed) means a summary or secondary source. UNVERIFIED (dotted) means memory or one weak source: test before relying on it.

docs.title: Eyes mode
docs.text:
Hunt · practice · 5 to 100 light curves

The story

In the first six quarters of Kepler data, volunteers on a website called Planet Hunters found a planet by looking at light curves by eye. It crosses the larger of two stars, which circle each other every 20 days, about once every 137 days, and it was named PH1 b LIKELY. A second pair of stars, about 1,000 times the Earth-Sun distance away, makes it the first transiting planet known in a four-star system LIKELY. Ahmed, that is why this book has an eyes mode: some planets have been found by people looking.

In plain words

You get a short stretch of real light curve with nothing marked on it. Say Dip, No dip, Odd or Not sure, and then the answer is shown. It is practice: the dips are fake planets we hid, plus glitches and real eclipses that we know about.

With JavaScript on, this spot is a practice game: you look at short stretches of the real TOI-1338 light curve and say whether you see a dip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Blind first. Nothing is marked until you answer, then the hidden thing is outlined.
  • Four answers. Dip is a planet-like dip that comes back up. No dip means nothing there. Odd is something that is not a planet: an eclipse, a spike or a sudden jump. Not sure is always allowed, and it is honest.
  • Keys. On a keyboard, press 1 to 4 to answer and Enter for the next one.
  • You choose the length of each sitting: 5, 20, 50 or 100 light curves.
  • Practice only. Every stretch comes from the real TOI-1338 light curve (TESS sector 98) with answers we know. The real stars of the hunt are not in here: they wait until you say start.
  • Looking exercise. This page has no text version, because the skill is seeing the picture. The light-curve explorer in Chapter 2 and the numbers in Chapter 7 cover the same ideas in words.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Every technical word in the book, in plain words. Pages link here the first time they use a term.

docs.title: Aperture
docs.text: The group of pixels whose light is added up to make a star's light curve. Choosing it well keeps the star's light in and the neighbours' light out. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: Arcsecond
docs.text: A tiny angle: 1/3,600 of a degree. A TESS pixel covers 21 arcseconds. Written ″; an arcminute (′) is 60 of them. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Binary star
docs.text: Two stars held together by gravity, each circling their shared centre. Our hunting ground: pairs where a planet might orbit both. See Chapter 4.

docs.title: Biweight filter
docs.text: A way to draw a smooth line through a light curve that ignores dips and outliers, so slow trends can be divided out without erasing a transit. Our detector uses a 2-day one. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: BTJD
docs.text: The TESS clock, in days: Barycentric Julian Date minus 2,457,000. BTJD 4025.6 is 16 December 2025.

docs.title: Cadence
docs.text: One measurement in a light curve, or the time between measurements: 2 minutes for SPOC light curves, 200 seconds for today's full-frame images.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text: A dip in a light curve that passed our first checks and might be a planet. Not a planet until professionals confirm it.

docs.title: CDPP
docs.text: "Combined Differential Photometric Precision": NASA's estimate of how much a star's brightness wobbles over a given time (like 1 hour), stored in each light-curve file. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Centroid
docs.text: The centre of a star's light on the camera, like the balance point of its pixels. If it shifts during a dip, the dip may come from a neighbour. See Chapter 10.

docs.title: Circumbinary planet
docs.text: A planet that orbits both stars of a pair. Its dips come at irregular times, which is why standard searches miss them. Our main quest.

docs.title: Critical orbit
docs.text: The closest a planet can orbit a pair of stars and stay stable: usually 2.5 to 3.5 times the stars' separation. See Chapter 4.

docs.title: CTOI
docs.text: Community TESS Object of Interest: a planet candidate found by a team outside NASA, posted on ExoFOP. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text: How much of the star's light a dip blocks, as a fraction: depth = (planet radius ÷ star radius)². Usually given in % or ppm.

docs.title: Detached binary
docs.text: Two stars far enough apart that they don't touch or distort each other; their eclipses look like clean, separate dips. Our G1 list keeps only these (Kepler's "morph" value below 0.5).

docs.title: Detrending
docs.text: Removing slow drifts (from the star or the spacecraft) so short dips stand out. We divide by a smooth fitted curve with a 2-day window. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Eclipsing binary
docs.text: Two stars orbiting each other, lined up so that one passes in front of the other. Makes deep, regular dips.

docs.title: ExoFOP
docs.text: The website where astronomers share follow-up information on TESS planet candidates. Since 2026 it asks for a published paper before accepting a community candidate. See Chapter 14.

docs.title: False alarm
docs.text: A "detection" caused by noise or spacecraft effects instead of a real dip. We count them by searching upside-down data.

docs.title: FITS
docs.text: The standard file format of astronomy since 1981: a header of labels plus tables or images. Every TESS file is FITS. See Lab 2.

docs.title: Full-frame image (FFI)
docs.text: A picture of a TESS camera's whole view, saved every 30 minutes, 10 minutes or 200 seconds depending on the year. Every star in view is in it. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: Gaia
docs.text: The European Space Agency's star-mapping spacecraft. Its catalogue gives positions, distances and colours for over a billion stars. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Injection test
docs.text: Hiding computer-made planet dips of known size in real data and checking how many the search finds. It measures what we can and can't detect.

docs.title: Kepler
docs.text: NASA's space telescope that stared at one patch of sky from 2009 to 2013 and found thousands of planets and eclipsing binaries. Our G1 stars come from its binary catalogue. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: KIC
docs.text: Kepler Input Catalog number: Kepler's ID for a star, like KIC 12644769 for Kepler-16.

docs.title: Light curve
docs.text: A star's brightness measured again and again over time and drawn as a graph: time along the bottom, brightness up the side.

docs.title: Look-elsewhere effect
docs.text: If you search in thousands of places, a few will show something unusual by chance. A search's false-alarm rate must count all its tries. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Magnitude
docs.text: Astronomy's brightness scale, where bigger numbers are fainter. 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: MAST
docs.text: The Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes: NASA's public archive holding all TESS and Kepler data. See Lab 1.

docs.title: Matched filter
docs.text: Sliding a template shaped like the signal you want (for us, a box-shaped dip) along the data and scoring how well each stretch matches.

docs.title: Momentum dump
docs.text: A short thruster firing that TESS uses every few days to stay pointed. It jolts the camera and can fake a dip; it's flagged in the data (quality bit 32). See Lab 2.

docs.title: N-body simulation
docs.text: A computer calculation that moves several objects (like two stars and a planet) step by step under each other's gravity. STANLEY uses one to predict when a two-star planet crosses.

docs.title: Parsec
docs.text: A distance of about 3.26 light years, used by astronomers. Kepler-16 is 75 parsecs away.

docs.title: PDCSAP and SAP
docs.text: Two versions of NASA's light curves. SAP is the raw light summed in the star's pixels; PDCSAP has known spacecraft effects removed.

docs.title: Phase fold
docs.text: Cutting a light curve into pieces one period long and stacking them, so repeating events (like eclipses) line up. Our eclipse mask finds eclipses this way.

docs.title: Photon noise
docs.text: The natural wobble in counting particles of light: like raindrops in a bucket, a count of N varies by about √N. It's the floor no instrument can beat. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: ppm
docs.text: Parts per million. 1% = 10,000 ppm. Earth crossing the Sun blocks about 84 ppm.

docs.title: Precession
docs.text: The slow turning of a planet's orbit around a pair of stars. It makes transits switch on and off over years. See Chapter 5.

docs.title: QLP
docs.text: MIT's Quick-Look Pipeline: makes light curves from full-frame images for a huge number of stars. All 549 G1 stars have QLP data. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: Quality flag
docs.text: A number stored with each measurement that warns about problems (thruster firing, scattered light...). 0 means fine. See Lab 2.

docs.title: RA and Dec
docs.text: The sky's longitude (Right Ascension) and latitude (Declination). Every star's address. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Radius
docs.text: Distance from the centre of a star or planet to its edge. We measure planets in Earth radii and stars in Sun radii (the Sun is about 109 Earths wide).

docs.title: Red noise
docs.text: Slow wobbles where neighbouring measurements move together. Unlike random noise, it doesn't shrink much when you average, so it fakes planet-like dips. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Robust spread
docs.text: A measure of wobble that ignores a few wild points: 1.4826 times the median distance from the median. Our detector uses it everywhere. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Scattered light
docs.text: Sunlight bounced off Earth or the Moon into TESS's cameras, raising the background. It creates slow ramps and fake dips, usually near the ends of each orbit.

docs.title: Secondary eclipse
docs.text: When the brighter star passes in front of the fainter one: a shallower dip than the primary eclipse, at another point in the binary's orbit.

docs.title: Sector
docs.text: One TESS stretch of about 27 days looking at the same patch of sky.

docs.title: SNR
docs.text: Signal-to-noise ratio: how big a signal is compared with normal wobble. SNR 7 means seven times the normal wobble. Our detection bar is 7.

docs.title: SPOC
docs.text: NASA's Science Processing Operations Center: makes the cleanest TESS light curves, from 2-minute postage stamps. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: STANLEY
docs.text: A search tool by David Martin's group (Martin et al. 2021) that looks for two-star planets by simulating orbits and stacking all their predicted crossings together. Installed on your PC.

docs.title: TESS
docs.text: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018. It photographs most of the sky, one sector at a time. All its data is free.

docs.title: TIC
docs.text: TESS Input Catalog number: TESS's ID for a star, like TIC 299096355 for Kepler-16. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: TOI
docs.text: TESS Object of Interest: a signal NASA's team thinks might be a planet. TOI-1338 became TOI-1338 b once confirmed.

docs.title: Transit
docs.text: A planet passing in front of its star as seen from Earth, which makes a small dip in the light curve.

docs.title: Virtual environment
docs.text: A private copy of Python with its own toolkits, kept inside a project folder so it doesn't clash with anything else. Ours is D:\second-sun\.venv. See Lab 0.

docs.title: White noise
docs.text: Random wobble where each measurement is independent. Averaging N measurements shrinks it by √N. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Progress
docs.text: A quiet record of where you are, Ahmed. It updates when we commit a change to the progress/ files, so the history is also in git.

docs.title: 1. Stars, names and missions
docs.text:
Chapter 1 · about 20 min · Maths: powers of ten, one logarithm (explained)

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. One star, three catalogues, three numbers: Kepler-16.KIC 12644769TIC 299096355Gaia DR3Kepler-16one starOne star, three catalogues, three numbers: Kepler-16.

1-minute summary

  • What: how stars get catalogue numbers, a position, a brightness and a distance, and which two telescopes matter.
  • Why: a number from one catalogue will not find a star in another, so every lookup needs the right name.
  • You will be able to: look up any star yourself and read its brightness, distance and TESS time.

The story

Ahmed, on 20 October you typed one name, Kepler-16, and the script answered with a pile of others: TIC 299096355, KIC 12644769 and Gaia DR3 2133476355197071616. One star, three catalogues, three numbers, 75 parsecs away and shining at TESS magnitude 10.94 VERIFIED. Each telescope team numbered the sky its own way, and nobody lined the numbers up for us. Before you can ask a star a question, you have to learn what each team calls it. That is this chapter.

In plain words

Every star we study has several catalogue numbers, a position, a brightness and a distance. Two space telescopes matter to us: Kepler, which stared at one patch of sky, and TESS, which sweeps the whole sky.

What this chapter answers: who watched these stars, how do we name them, and how do we read their numbers?

docs.title: 1.1 The intuition
docs.text:
Think of a house in Kuwait City. It has a street address, a block number, a civil ID number on the land registry, and maybe a name the family calls it. Four labels, one house. Each label comes from a different office, made for a different job.

Stars are the same. Kepler-16 is the name its discoverers gave it. KIC 12644769 is its number in Kepler's catalogue. TIC 299096355 is its number in TESS's catalogue. Gaia DR3 2133476355197071616 is its number in the European star map VERIFIED. One star, four offices.

docs.title: How planets around other stars are found
docs.text:
Method What you see Who uses it Transit the star dims when a planet passes in front Kepler, TESS, us Radial velocity the star wobbles toward and away from us, shifting its colour slightly big ground telescopes Timing a regular clock (eclipses, a pulsar) runs early and late as a planet tugs on it used for some two-star planets Imaging a photo of the planet itself only for big, young planets far from their star

We use transits because they need only a brightness measurement, which is exactly what TESS gives away for free.

docs.title: The two telescopes
docs.text:
Kepler (NASA, 2009 to 2013 for its main mission) stared at one patch of sky of 105 square degrees, about 500 times the area of the full Moon, in the constellations Cygnus and Lyra. It watched about 200,000 objects almost without a break LIKELY. Because it never looked away, it caught thousands of eclipsing binaries: pairs of stars that pass in front of each other. A team at Villanova University keeps the catalogue of them: 2,921 rows in the version we downloaded VERIFIED.

TESS (NASA, launched 2018) does the opposite: it sweeps almost the whole sky, one strip at a time. It circles Earth every 13.7 days, has 4 cameras, and watches each patch for about a month; stars near the poles of its sweep get up to a year LIKELY VERIFIED. Its pixels are big, 21 arcseconds each LIKELY, which matters a lot in Chapter 11.

Why both matter to us: Kepler found the binaries and timed their eclipses precisely. TESS is now re-watching many of them, years later. Our G1 campaign searches TESS data of Kepler's binaries (Chapter 5 explains why the years in between help).

docs.title: The catalogues
docs.text: Catalogue Made by What it holds Example KIC (Kepler Input Catalog) Kepler team the stars Kepler could watch KIC 12644769 Kepler EB catalogue Villanova Kepler's eclipsing binaries, with their periods our G1 source TIC (TESS Input Catalog) TESS team, built on Gaia LIKELY about every star TESS can see, with brightness, size, distance TIC 299096355 Gaia DR3 European Space Agency positions and distances of over a billion stars; detailed values for about 470 million LIKELY Gaia DR3 2133... TOI (TESS Object of Interest) TESS team signals NASA thinks might be planets; 2,241 from the first two years LIKELY TOI-1338 CTOI (Community TOI) anyone, via ExoFOP candidates found by outside teams, like us one day none of ours yet

docs.title: How planets get their names
docs.text: A star system's planets get lowercase letters in order of discovery, starting at b ("a" is never used for a planet). TOI-1338 started as TOI-1338.01, a "maybe". Once it was confirmed as a planet it became TOI-1338 b. In a two-star system the stars are A (the brighter one) and B, and a planet orbiting both is sometimes written (AB) b.

docs.title: Position: RA and Dec
docs.text:
The sky is treated as a giant ball around Earth. Declination (Dec) is latitude: +90° is above the North Pole, 0° is above the equator. Right Ascension (RA) is longitude, measured eastward, in degrees (0 to 360) or in hours (0 to 24, with 1 hour = 15°). Kepler-16 sits at RA 289.08°, Dec +51.76°.

Small angles use arcminutes (′) and arcseconds (″): 1° = 60′ = 3,600″. The full Moon is about 30′ across. A TESS pixel is 21″, so about 90 of them fit across the Moon.

docs.title: Brightness: magnitudes
docs.text:
Astronomers measure brightness backwards: bigger numbers mean fainter. The scale is a logarithm, so each step multiplies:

m1 − m2 = −2.5 log10(F1 / F2)

  • m: magnitude. F: the light we receive (flux).
  • A logarithm answers "10 to what power?": log10(100) = 2.
  • So 5 magnitudes = a factor of 100 in brightness, and 1 magnitude is a factor of about 2.5.

Worked through: your eyes reach about magnitude 6 on a dark night. Kepler-16 is 10.94, about 5 magnitudes fainter: roughly 100 times too faint to see. Our faintest G1 stars are 13.5, about 2.6 magnitudes, or 11 times, fainter than Kepler-16. Fainter means fewer photons, which means more noise (Chapter 7).

TESS magnitude (Tmag) is measured through TESS's red filter, so it differs a little from the magnitudes in other catalogues.

docs.title: Distance: parsecs
docs.text: A parsec is about 3.26 light years. Gaia measures distances by watching each star shift slightly as Earth goes around the Sun (parallax). Kepler-16 is 75 parsecs away VERIFIED: about 245 light years. The light we measured in 2024 left it around the year 1780.

docs.title: Time: BJD and BTJD
docs.text: Light from a star reaches the Sun and Earth at slightly different moments, up to about 8 minutes apart. So astronomers convert every time to when the light would have reached the Sun's centre of mass (the solar system's balance point): the Barycentric Julian Date (BJD), a count of days. Those numbers are huge (2,460,000 and more), so TESS subtracts 2,457,000: BTJD. BTJD 0 is 8 December 2014. Kepler's catalogue uses a different offset (BJD − 2,400,000), which is why our G1 list has times like 55002.78.

docs.title: 1.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
The G1 list, targets/g1_targets.csv, is the catalogue work done once and frozen:

Column Meaning From kic Kepler's number Villanova catalogue tic TESS's number looked up in the TIC at MAST tmag TESS magnitude TIC p_bin_d how many days the two stars take to orbit each other Villanova bjd0 the time of one eclipse (BJD − 2,400,000) Villanova morph 0 = clean, separate eclipses; 1 = stars touching Villanova

The selection rule keeps morph < 0.5 (stars clearly separate), p_bin_d > 5 days (room for a stable planet, Chapter 4) and tmag ≤ 13.5 (bright enough to see a planet). That leaves 552 rows: 549 stars, because 3 stars have two binary periods each VERIFIED.

Found on 20 October: a hole in the rule

Kepler's catalogue writes morph = −1 when it couldn't measure a binary's shape. "−1 < 0.5" is true, so our rule let those stars in: 136 of the 552 rows VERIFIED. One of them showed no eclipse at all in TESS data. Lesson: a "missing value" code inside a number column must be handled on purpose. The fix is your decision when the hunt resumes; it's in the decision log.

The top of the file records the fingerprints (sha256) of the source files, so anyone can check the list wasn't changed.

docs.title: 1.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• We can: find any star's numbers, brightness, distance and available data in under a minute.
  • We can't: fully trust catalogue values for binaries. The TIC treats Kepler-16 as one star of 4018 K, but the light is a blend of two stars. Sizes and temperatures for our G1 stars are blended guesses.
  • Names are pointers, not facts. A star with a TOI number is not a planet host until confirmed.

docs.title: 2. Light curves: seeing planets as shadows
docs.text:
Chapter 2 · about 25 min · Maths: fractions, percentages, ppm, squares, averages

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Two kinds of dip in a light curve.eclipse: deepplanet: shallowbrightnesstimeTwo kinds of dip in a light curve.

1-minute summary

  • What: a light curve is brightness against time, and a planet crossing its star makes a small dip called a transit.
  • Why: we cannot photograph these planets, so dips are our only view of them.
  • You will be able to: tell a transit from an eclipse by its shape and size.

The story

Fold TOI-1338's light on its 14.6-day star orbit and one sun passing in front of the other drops the light by about 6% VERIFIED. The planet's crossing, five hours long, dims it by only about 0.2% VERIFIED. Both are dips, and only one is a planet. A light curve is the page where you learn to tell them apart, and it is the page we will be reading for the rest of this book.

In plain words

We cannot photograph these planets, so we watch a star's brightness over time. When a planet passes in front, the star dims a little: that is a transit.

What this chapter answers: how does a brightness graph reveal a planet, and how does the TESS telescope collect that graph?

docs.title: 2.1 The intuition
docs.text:
Stand at night and look at a distant streetlight. A moth flies across it. You can't see the moth, but for a moment the light looks a touch dimmer. If you'd been measuring the light with a meter every few seconds, you'd see a small notch in the readings. The size of the notch tells you how big the moth is compared with the lamp.

The star is the lamp. The planet is the moth. TESS is the meter.

docs.title: 2.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
A light curve is a list of (time, brightness) pairs. For a star with no planet and no partner, it's roughly flat, with random jitter (noise). A transit shows as a dip with a flat bottom: the planet slides on, sits fully in front, slides off.

Three numbers describe a transit:

Number Meaning What it tells us Depth how much dimmer the star gets the planet's size compared with the star Duration how long the dip lasts how fast the planet moves across, and the path it takes Time (mid-point) when it happens for single-star planets, the period; for two-sun planets, a timing pattern (Chapter 5)

docs.title: Depth and size
docs.text:
The planet blocks a disc of light. The fraction blocked is the planet's disc area divided by the star's disc area. Area grows with radius squared, so VERIFIED:

depth ≈ (Rp / R★)²

  • Rp: the planet's radius (centre to edge).
  • R★: the star's radius.

Depths are tiny, so we use ppm (parts per million): 1% = 10,000 ppm. Earth crossing the Sun: (1/109)² ≈ 0.000084 = 84 ppm. Jupiter crossing the Sun: about 1% = 10,000 ppm.

Turning it around gives the planet's size from a measured depth: Rp = R★ × √depth.

docs.title: How TESS collects light curves
docs.text:
TESS is a NASA space telescope that stares at one big patch of sky for about 27 days (a sector), then moves on VERIFIED. It records brightness two ways:

  • Full-frame images of the whole patch: every 30 minutes (sectors 1-26), every 10 minutes (27-55), every 200 seconds (56 onward) VERIFIED.
  • 2-minute "postage stamps" for selected stars, which NASA's SPOC pipeline turns into ready-made light curves. Most of our tests use these.

The SPOC light curves come in two versions you'll meet in our code:

  • SAP (simple aperture photometry): the raw sum of light in the star's pixels.
  • PDCSAP: SAP with known spacecraft effects removed. Cleaner, but occasionally missing data where SAP is fine. Detector v2 fills those gaps from SAP (Chapter 8).

docs.title: Noise
docs.text: Every measurement jitters. For a star like TOI-1338 (TESS magnitude about 11.5), one hour of 2-minute data scatters by roughly 400 to 550 ppm in our measurements (overnight test, pipeline/diag_v2_results.json). A planet's dip has to stand clearly above that, which is the subject of Chapter 8.

docs.title: 2.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
In pipeline/detect_v2.py, the function load(path):

  1. reads a SPOC light-curve file with lightkurve, dropping cadences flagged as bad ("hard" quality mask);
  2. divides by the median so "normal brightness" = 1.0;
  3. fills PDCSAP gaps from SAP, scaled to match nearby data;
  4. returns t (time in BTJD, the TESS day count) and f (relative flux).

BTJD = BJD − 2,457,000. For example, BTJD 4025.6 is 16 December 2025.

docs.title: 2.5 Worked example: two kinds of dip in TOI-1338
docs.text:
TOI-1338's light curve shows dips of very different sizes:

Dip Depth Cause Primary eclipse, every 14.6 days about 6% at the bottom, 5.7% typical inside it VERIFIED the small star passes in front of the big one Secondary eclipse about 0.3% VERIFIED the big star covers the small one 16 Dec 2025, once about 0.24% (2,400 ppm), ~6.4 h the planet TOI-1338 b VERIFIED

With JavaScript on, this spot shows the real TOI-1338 light curve for sector 98, which you can drag and zoom.

Try it. This is the real light curve from our own run (TESS sector 98, averaged into 10-minute steps). Press Whole sector and count the deep eclipses. Then press Planet crossing and look at the dip that is roughly thirty times shallower. Drag the picture to move along it, or use the buttons.

Check the planet with the formula: TOI-1338 b is about 6.9 Earth radii VERIFIED, and the big star is about 1.3 Sun radii (the value used in our injection test). In Earth radii the star is 1.3 × 109 ≈ 142. So depth ≈ (6.9 / 142)² ≈ 0.0024 = 2,400 ppm. That matches what our search measured.

docs.title: 2.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• A dip is not a planet. Spacecraft effects, star spots, the other star, or a faint background binary can all make dips. Chapter 8 and the vetting chapter deal with that.
  • Depth gives a size only relative to the star. If the star's size is wrong, or another star's light dilutes the dip, the planet size is wrong too.
  • One sector is a short window. Two-sun planets often cross only once per sector or not at all, which is why the next chapter matters.

docs.title: 3. Our data: from a NASA telescope to your D: drive
docs.text:
Chapter 3 · about 20 min · Maths: megabytes and gigabytes, ppm

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. From a camera in orbit to a file on your PC.TESS camerain orbitNASA pipelinecleans itMAST archivefree onlineYour D: driveour codeFrom a camera in orbit to a file on your PC.

1-minute summary

  • What: the path from TESS's camera to a file on your D: drive, and what can go wrong on the way.
  • Why: every number in this book starts here, so the data's limits are our limits.
  • You will be able to: name the data products we use, how big they are and how good.

The story

Kepler-16's file for sector 82 holds 18,619 measurements spread over 25.9 days, and the whole file is 1.9 MB VERIFIED. A month of one star's life in under two megabytes. Of those measurements, 482 carry a warning flag, and 16 of the flags mark the moments TESS fired its thrusters. The data is tiny and generous, but it comes with warnings, and learning to read them is what this chapter is for.

In plain words

NASA turns TESS pictures into brightness records and puts them online for free, and our code downloads them to your D: drive. This chapter follows that path so you know what our data is and what can go wrong with it.

What this chapter answers: what data do we use, how does it reach your PC, and how good is it?

docs.title: 3.1 The intuition
docs.text: Think of a security camera that photographs a whole car park every few minutes. Later, someone goes through the photos and, for each parked car, writes down how bright its headlights looked in each photo. You get the notebook, not the photos. That notebook is a light curve. If you ever need to check something the notebook can't tell you, you can go back to the photos (the pixels).

docs.title: 3.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
TESS has 4 cameras, each seeing a 24 × 24 degree patch of sky, with 4 detector chips of 2048 × 2048 pixels each. One pixel covers about 21 arcseconds LIKELY. That's a big pixel: several stars can share one, which is why the "neighbour" test in Chapter 10 matters.

TESS circles Earth every 13.7 days and watches each patch for about 27 days (a sector). Stars near the ecliptic poles get watched for up to a year VERIFIED.

The data comes in three layers:

Layer What it is Size per star per sector (measured) VERIFIED When we use it Light curve (SPOC, QLP, TESS-SPOC) the brightness notebook, ready-made 0.7-2 MB almost always Target pixel file the small stack of pixels around one star, every cadence ~50 MB checking where a dip comes from (Chapter 10, C6) TESScut cutout a square of pixels cut from the full-frame images ~11-50 MB faint stars with no ready-made light curve

Your rule from 19 October: we keep light curves, but cutouts are deleted after we extract what we need, because NASA keeps the originals.

docs.title: From pixels to a light curve
docs.text:
TESS doesn't send home "light curves". It sends pictures, and teams on the ground turn them into brightness lists:

  1. Postage stamps. For a limited set of chosen stars, TESS keeps a small square of pixels every 2 minutes (some every 20 seconds). These are target pixel files.
  2. Full-frame images (FFIs). The whole camera view, saved every 30 minutes in the first two years, every 10 minutes later, and every 200 seconds now VERIFIED. Every star in view is in them, but at a slower rhythm.
  3. Photometry. A team picks which pixels belong to a star (the aperture), adds up their light every cadence, subtracts the background sky, and cleans out spacecraft effects. The result is the light curve you downloaded in Lab 2.

docs.title: Who makes the light curves
docs.text:
All of it lives at MAST (the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes), NASA's public archive. For Kepler-16 alone, MAST holds 94 light curves from six teams VERIFIED:

Team Made from Rhythm Notes SPOC (NASA Ames) postage stamps 2 min (some 20 s) the cleanest; our first choice TESS-SPOC FFIs FFI rhythm SPOC's method on many more stars QLP (MIT Quick-Look Pipeline) FFIs FFI rhythm the widest coverage: every G1 star has it TARS, CDIPS, TASOC FFIs FFI rhythm other science teams' versions; useful for second opinions

In our G1 list, QLP covers all 549 stars, SPOC 275 and TESS-SPOC 312 VERIFIED. They're made independently, which is why rule C8 (Chapter 10) asks for a dip in at least two of them.

docs.title: Where they land on your PC
docs.text: Every download goes under D:\second-sun\data\ (never C:), into a mastDownload folder that copies MAST's own layout, and gets a line in research/downloads.csv. You did this yourself in Lab 2.

docs.title: How good is the data?
docs.text:
On Kepler-16, a fairly bright star in our G1 field (TESS magnitude 10.94), a quick estimate of one hour's scatter gives 236 ppm (SPOC), 279 ppm (TESS-SPOC) or 293 ppm (QLP) VERIFIED. Those three numbers are good for comparing the products: SPOC is the quietest.

Correction, 20 October 2026

That quick estimate flattens the light curve with a window only 3.4 hours long, which removes the slow wobble that matters for our multi-hour transits. Measured the way our detector sees the data, the same hour scatters by about 900 ppm; NASA's own estimate is 542 ppm VERIFIED. The optimistic number was one reason for an early overstatement of how small a planet we could find. Chapter 7 explains why the method changes the answer.

docs.title: Known troublemakers in the data
docs.text:
• Momentum dumps: every 2-6 days TESS fires thrusters; the cadences are flagged (quality bit 32) LIKELY. Chapter 8 showed fakes cluster near them.
  • Data gaps: downlinks to Earth every orbit leave holes; edges of holes are where detrending goes wrong.
  • Scattered light from the Earth and Moon near the ends of orbits.

docs.title: 3.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
• Downloads use lightkurve (a Python package), always into D:\second-sun\data\ or D:\second-sun\.cache\, never C:.
  • Every download is logged in research/downloads.csv (what, from where, size, why).
  • Your PC's Avast antivirus intercepts secure web connections. Python is told to trust the Windows certificate list (a package called truststore), inside the project only. Avast itself is untouched.
  • Third-party tools get checked first. On 20 October, STANLEY tried to download to C:; it was caught before any file landed, and now a wrapper forces its downloads onto D: (logged in the mistakes register).

docs.title: 3.5 Worked example: what it cost to test STANLEY on TOI-1338
docs.text: TOI-1338 sits near the south ecliptic pole, so TESS has watched it a lot: 40 sectors of 2-minute data. At about 2 MB each, that's 78 MB in total, which is small. The same star as raw cutouts would be roughly 40 × 30 MB ≈ 1.2 GB. That gap is why we prefer ready-made light curves.

docs.title: 3.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• The data is free and reachable from your PC, and light curves are small enough that even hundreds of stars fit easily on D:.
  • A light curve hides choices. Each pipeline cleaned the data its own way. A dip in only one product could be that product's artefact.
  • Big pixels mean blends. A dip can come from a neighbour inside the same 21-arcsecond pixel. Light curves alone can't rule that out; pixels can.

docs.title: 4. Two suns: binary stars and the planets around them
docs.text:
Chapter 4 · about 20 min · Maths: ratios, powers (squares, cubes, square roots)

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. A planet circling two suns.planettwo suns, one planet around bothA planet circling two suns.

1-minute summary

  • What: binary stars, and the planets that orbit both stars at once.
  • Why: only 14 have ever been seen crossing their stars, so each new one matters. VERIFIED
  • You will be able to: explain what a circumbinary planet is and why we hunt them.

The story

Kepler-16 b, found in 2011, was the first planet seen crossing in front of two stars: a Saturn-like world that circles a pair of suns once every 229 days or so LIKELY. Since then only 14 have ever been caught this way VERIFIED. Ahmed, that is why we are here. A club this small notices every new member.

In plain words

Many stars come in pairs, and a planet can orbit both at once. Only 14 such planets have ever been caught crossing their stars, so every new one matters. VERIFIED

What this chapter answers: what is a circumbinary planet, and where around a pair of stars can one survive?

docs.title: 4.1 The intuition
docs.text:
Picture two dancers spinning around each other in the middle of a room, holding hands. Now picture a child running in a big circle around both of them. If the child runs too close, the dancers' swinging arms knock them off course. If the child stays far enough out, the dancers just feel like one big blur in the middle, and the child can run in circles forever.

That's a circumbinary planet. The two dancers are the stars. The child is the planet. "Too close" is a real, measurable distance, and the known planets sit just outside it.

docs.title: 4.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
A binary star is two stars bound by gravity, each orbiting their shared centre of mass. Astronomers describe a binary with:

  • its period: how long the stars take to go around each other once (days for the pairs we study);
  • its separation: how far apart they are (written abin);
  • its eccentricity e: how stretched the orbit is (0 = a circle, closer to 1 = a long thin oval);
  • its mass ratio μ: the smaller star's share of the total mass.

A planet can orbit in two ways:

Type Orbits Example S-type (circumstellar) one of the two stars, with the other far away many planets in wide binaries P-type (circumbinary) both stars together Kepler-16 b, TOI-1338 b

We hunt the P-type. The first one caught transiting was Kepler-16 b in 2011, a Saturn-like planet on a ~229-day orbit around a pair of stars that circle each other every 41 days LIKELY. Since then, only 14 transiting circumbinary planets are known: 12 from Kepler and 2 from TESS VERIFIED.

docs.title: How close can a planet get?
docs.text:
Too close to the pair, the stars' changing pull throws the planet out. Holman and Wiegert ran thousands of simulated orbits and fitted a formula for the closest stable distance, ac VERIFIED:

ac / abin = 1.60 + 5.10 e − 2.22 e² + 4.12 μ − 4.27 e μ − 5.09 μ² + 4.61 e² μ²

Every symbol, one by one:

  • ac: the critical (closest stable) distance of the planet from the pair's centre.
  • abin: the separation of the two stars.
  • e: the binary's eccentricity (0 to about 0.7 for this formula).
  • μ = m2 / (m1 + m2): the mass ratio, the small star's mass m2 divided by the total (0.1 to 0.5 for this formula).

You don't need to memorise it. The lesson is in the result: for the known systems, ac comes out at 2.5 to 3.5 times the stars' separation VERIFIED.

docs.title: From distance to time: Kepler's third law
docs.text:
We measure periods (time), not distances. Kepler's third law links them: for orbits around the same mass, period² ∝ distance³. So the ratio of two periods is the ratio of two distances raised to the power 3/2:

Pc / Pbin ≈ (ac / abin)3/2

"Raised to the power 3/2" means: cube it, then take the square root. For a distance ratio of 3: 3³ = 27, and √27 ≈ 5.2. So a planet at 3 times the separation takes about 5 times as long as the binary to go round. Across the known systems the critical period is 4 to 7 times the binary period VERIFIED.

docs.title: The pile-up
docs.text: The innermost known planets sit just outside the danger zone, at only 1.3 to 1.6 times the critical period VERIFIED. Nature seems to park them right at the edge. That's useful: when we see a pair of stars with a 15-day period, we know roughly where to expect a planet (around 60 to 120 days).

docs.title: 4.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
This chapter's ideas become a search window in the pipeline. For each G1 binary:

  1. Read its period and eccentricity from the Kepler eclipsing-binary catalogue (wave 1c).
  2. Compute the critical period from the formula above.
  3. Treat planets from about 1 to 10 times that period as the most likely, without throwing away anything outside it.

The formula is coded in pipeline/stability.py (about 30 lines). Its function critical(e, mu) returns the critical distance ratio, the critical period ratio, and whether e and μ are inside the range the fit was made for; search_window(p_bin, e, m1, m2) turns that into a range of planet periods to search. Running python stability.py checks it against TOI-1338 (next section). Status: VERIFIED (self-check passes).

docs.title: 4.5 Worked example: TOI-1338
docs.text:
TOI-1338 is a pair of stars (about 1.1 and 0.3 times the Sun's mass) that orbit each other every 14.6 days with eccentricity 0.16. Its planet, TOI-1338 b, goes around both every 95.2 days and is about 6.9 times Earth's size VERIFIED.

  • Critical period: about 4.9 × 14.6 days ≈ 72 days (the 4.9 comes from the Holman-Wiegert formula with this star's e and μ; wave 1a, claim C2).
  • Planet's period: 95.2 days.
  • Ratio: 95.2 ÷ 72 ≈ 1.3. Just outside the edge, exactly like the pile-up says VERIFIED.

This is the star our tools have practised on. In Chapter 8 you'll see our search find one of its crossings in December 2025.

docs.title: 4.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• It lets us predict where planets are most likely, and recognise that a "planet" closer than the critical period is suspicious.
  • It doesn't tell us whether a planet exists. Most pairs may have none, and the formula is a fit to simulations with limits (e up to ~0.7, μ from 0.1 to 0.5).
  • Fourteen planets is a tiny sample. Patterns like the pile-up could partly reflect how we search. Papers argue it's real (Martin 2018), but keep the doubt in mind.

docs.title: 5. Why two-sun transits wander
docs.text:
Chapter 5 · about 25 min · Maths: averages, rough speeds, percentages

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Crossings that miss the clock.93 days95 days88 daysgrey: where a clock would put the dipsCrossings that miss the clock.

1-minute summary

  • What: why a two-sun planet's dips come early, late, longer or shorter.
  • Why: that wandering hides them from normal search tools, which is our chance.
  • You will be able to: say why a search that expects a steady clock misses them.

The story

TOI-1338 b is no clock. Its first three crossings came about 93 and 95 days apart, and lasted about 0.3, 0.4 and 0.6 days VERIFIED. Worse for anyone searching, its orbit slowly tilts, so it swings in and out of view over 21.4 years VERIFIED. A planet that is late, a different shape each time and sometimes absent: that is what wandering means, and it is why a search that expects a steady beat misses it.

In plain words

Around one star, a planet's dips arrive like a clock. Around two moving stars they do not, which makes these planets hard to find and gives our hunt its chance.

What this chapter answers: why are circumbinary transits irregular, and how does that create our G1 opportunity?

docs.title: 5.1 The intuition
docs.text:
Imagine a lighthouse on a boat, and the boat is circling in the harbour. You walk around the harbour on a path. Each time you pass in front of the lighthouse beam, the boat is somewhere different on its circle. Sometimes you meet it early, sometimes late. If the boat is moving the same way you are, you stay in its beam longer; if it moves the opposite way, you flash past.

The boat is the star being crossed. You're the planet.

With JavaScript on, this spot shows two stars circling each other and a planet circling both, with the brightness plotted underneath. The planet's crossings come at uneven gaps.

Try it. Press Play, or drag Time. The grey line is the two stars passing in front of each other, and it keeps a steady beat. The amber line is the planet's dips, and they do not: the gaps and the lengths change, and some crossings can be missing altogether. Change the planet's year and watch the gaps change. The picture is not to scale: the planet is drawn far too big so that its dip shows, and the orbits are drawn as circles.

docs.title: 5.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
Three effects make circumbinary transits irregular:

  1. Timing shifts. Each star swings around the pair's centre. The planet crosses the star wherever the star happens to be, so the gaps between transits vary. These shifts can be days, longer than a transit lasts, so the usual trick of folding the data at one period fails. Every Kepler circumbinary discovery was made by eye VERIFIED.
  2. Duration changes. If the star moves the same direction as the planet, the crossing is slow and long; the opposite direction makes it short. TOI-1338 b's first three TESS transits came about 93 and 95 days apart and lasted about 0.3, 0.4 and 0.6 days VERIFIED.
  3. Switching on and off. The planet's orbit slowly tilts around (it precesses). For part of each cycle it's lined up to cross the stars; for the rest it misses them completely. Kepler-453 b crosses only about 8% of the time: for every one like it we see, about 12 are hidden right now LIKELY.

docs.title: Precession and transit windows
docs.text:
The two stars aren't a perfect point mass, so they pull the planet's orbit plane round in a slow circle. Call the time for one full turn the precession period. For TOI-1338 b it's 21.4 years VERIFIED. Transits are only possible while the planet's orbit plane cuts across the stars, so they come in windows separated by long silences.

Kostov et al. (2020) worked out that TOI-1338 b's transits would become unlikely, with at most about a 30% chance per crossing, after 12 September 2025 VERIFIED. Yet a 2024 model by Wang and Liu predicted one specific crossing on 16 December 2025, and our search found a dip that same night VERIFIED. The "30%" was a chance, not a ban: this was one of the crossings that happened.

docs.title: Why normal searches miss them
docs.text: NASA's SPOC pipeline flags a planet only after it sees at least two transits and a detection score above 7.1 LIKELY. Its multi-transit method assumes a fixed period. A two-sun planet with shifting timing, changing durations, and one transit per sector can slip through.

docs.title: 5.4 Our implementation: the G1 idea
docs.text:
From 2009 to 2013 the Kepler telescope stared at one patch of sky and catalogued about 2,900 eclipsing binaries. Kepler's planets were found in that window. But precession means some planets that were not crossing back then could be crossing now. A 2017 study estimated Kepler's binaries hold about 17 to 30 more such planets that will start transiting someday, possibly during TESS LIKELY.

TESS has re-observed the Kepler field. G1 is the search of those binaries in the newer TESS data. In code this means:

  • take the Kepler binary's period and eclipse times from the catalogue;
  • mask its eclipses (Chapter 8);
  • search what's left for single dips, and later for groups of dips that fit a circumbinary orbit.

docs.title: 5.5 Worked example: TOI-1338 b's timeline
docs.text:
When What happened Source 2018-2019 (sectors 3, 6, 10) first three transits, 93 and 95 days apart, 0.3-0.6 d long VERIFIED 2020 planet announced; precession period 21.4 yr; transits predicted to become rare after Sep 2025 VERIFIED 2024 Wang and Liu predict a crossing on 16 Dec 2025, 02:13 UTC, 6.31 h VERIFIED 16 Dec 2025 our search finds a 0.24% dip that night, about 1 hour after the predicted time VERIFIED

That one-hour difference is bigger than the paper's stated error (±23 min). It could be real wobble, or our timing error could be bigger than it looks. We haven't measured our error carefully yet (not measured yet; it's on the task list). A known planet's crossing that nobody has published yet is a nice result for practice, but it is not a discovery.

docs.title: 5.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• It explains why there's room for us: standard tools are built for clockwork planets.
  • It doesn't promise planets. The 17-30 estimate is a model, and many of those planets could be small or faint.
  • Irregular timing cuts both ways. It hides planets from NASA's pipeline, but it also means one dip alone is weak evidence. A strong case needs dips that fit a physical orbit around the two stars.

docs.title: 6. Orbits and the three-body problem
docs.text:
Chapter 6 · about 20 min · Maths: squares, cubes, cube roots, speeds

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. The planet keeps outside the unstable zone.planet's orbittoo close:unstablestarsThe planet keeps outside the unstable zone.

1-minute summary

  • What: Kepler's law, the closest safe orbit, and why three pulling bodies have no simple formula.
  • Why: a computer has to step through the motion, and that is what STANLEY does.
  • You will be able to: read a crossing's time and length as a clue to where the stars were.

The story

TOI-1338 b circles two suns of about 1.1 and 0.3 times ours every 95.2 days, while the suns circle each other every 14.6 VERIFIED. It sits only 1.34 times the closest period where an orbit stays safe VERIFIED. Any closer and the stars would likely throw it out. Nobody can write one tidy formula for three bodies pulling on each other, so a computer has to move them forward in tiny steps, and that is the trick behind STANLEY.

In plain words

Two stars circle their shared balance point and a planet circles both. Three bodies have no simple formula, so a computer moves them step by step.

What this chapter answers: how do orbits work, why can't we just write down when a two-star planet will cross, and how far from the stars can a planet survive?

docs.title: 6.1 The intuition
docs.text:
Two dancers hold hands and spin. They turn around a point between them, closer to the heavier dancer. A third dancer jogs in a big circle around both. Each time the jogger passes the front of the room, one of the spinners is somewhere different: sometimes in front, sometimes behind, sometimes moving the same way as the jogger, sometimes the opposite way.

If you were timing "jogger passes spinner A", your times would jump around, and how long the jogger stays in front of A would change too. That's a two-star planet's transit.

docs.title: 6.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
• The balance point (barycentre). Two stars orbit their common centre of mass. The heavy star makes a small circle, the light star a big one.
  • Kepler's third law. The farther out an orbit, the longer it takes, in a fixed way that depends on the mass inside it (Eq. 6.1). Johannes Kepler found it in 1619; Newton explained it with gravity.
  • Eccentricity (e). How stretched an orbit is: 0 is a circle; TOI-1338's stars have e ≈ 0.16 LIKELY. In a stretched orbit the two eclipses are not half an orbit apart. In Lab 5 they're 0.453 apart VERIFIED.
  • The three-body problem. Two bodies: a neat formula (an ellipse) for all time. Three: no general formula exists. You calculate the forces, move everything a tiny step, and repeat. That's an N-body simulation.
  • Stability. Too close to the two stars, a planet gets thrown out or swallowed. Holman and Wiegert (1999) measured the closest safe distance with thousands of simulations VERIFIED. For known two-star planets it's 2.5 to 3.5 times the stars' separation VERIFIED, and many known planets sit just outside it VERIFIED.
  • Precession. The planet's orbit slowly wobbles like a spinning top, so its crossings switch on and off over years (LIKELY, Chapter 5).

docs.title: Kepler's third law
docs.text:
P² = a³ / M

  • P: orbital period in years; a: orbit size in AU (the Earth-Sun distance); M: total mass inside, in Suns.
  • TOI-1338's stars: P = 14.6 d = 0.0400 yr, M = 1.4 Suns. a³ = 1.4 × 0.0400² = 0.00224, so a = 0.131 AU.
  • Its planet: P = 95.2 d = 0.261 yr. a³ = 1.4 × 0.261² = 0.0951, so a = 0.457 AU: 3.5 times the stars' separation.

docs.title: The closest stable orbit
docs.text:
Holman and Wiegert give the critical distance ac as a formula in e and the mass ratio μ = mB / (mA + mB). Converting it to a period with Kepler's law:

Pc / Pbin = (ac / abin)1.5

  • For TOI-1338 (e = 0.16, μ = 0.21): ac / abin = 2.87, so Pc = 2.871.5 × 14.6 d = 71 days.
  • The planet's 95.2 days is 1.34 times that VERIFIED: close to the edge, like most known two-star planets.
  • For G1 this sets where to look: planets shorter than Pc can't exist, so the search starts there.

docs.title: Why crossing times and lengths change
docs.text:
A crossing lasts about (star's width) ÷ (planet's speed relative to the star). Both bodies are moving:

  • Star A's speed around the balance point: its orbit radius is 0.131 AU × (0.3 / 1.4) = 0.028 AU = 4.2 million km, covered in 14.6 days: about 21 km/s.
  • The planet's speed: 2π × 0.457 AU in 95.2 days: about 52 km/s.
  • Moving the same way: 52 − 21 = 31 km/s (a slow, long crossing). Opposite ways: 52 + 21 = 73 km/s (a fast, short one).

So one planet's crossings can differ in length by a factor of about 2. TOI-1338 b's first crossings lasted between about 0.3 and 0.6 days VERIFIED. And because star A is somewhere different on its little circle each time, the crossing time shifts by hours to days VERIFIED.

docs.title: An N-body simulation, step by step
docs.text:
1. Put the three bodies at their starting positions with their speeds.
  2. Work out the gravity force on each from the other two (Newton: force ∝ mass × mass ÷ distance²).
  3. Move every body a tiny time step, update speeds, repeat millions of times.
  4. Whenever the planet passes in front of a star along our line of sight, record the time and the length of the crossing.

Real codes like REBOUND (Rein and Liu 2012) use clever stepping rules that stay accurate over years. STANLEY uses REBOUND.

docs.title: 6.4 Our implementation
docs.text: Where What pipeline/stability.py critical(e, mu): the Holman-Wiegert formula. search_window(...): the planet periods worth searching for a binary. docs.title: 7. Noise and statistics: when is a dip real?
docs.text:
Chapter 7 · about 20 min · Maths: averages, square roots, one probability

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. A dip has to stand out from the scatter.a dip must stand out from the scatterA dip has to stand out from the scatter.

1-minute summary

  • What: noise, signal to noise (SNR), and how chance alone makes fake dips.
  • Why: a dip only counts if it is clearly bigger than the wobble over the same length of time.
  • You will be able to: say how sure a dip is, and why averaging does not fix slow drifts.

The story

To find out how often noise alone fools us, we turned TOI-1338's light curves upside down, so that no planet could be in them. Our detector still announced 6 dips in 10 sectors, one as strong as SNR 12.6 VERIFIED. Nothing was there. Noise is patient, and if you search enough places it will build you a planet. This chapter is how to tell the difference.

In plain words

Every measurement wobbles, and a dip only counts if it is clearly bigger than the wobble. Look in thousands of places and a few will fake a dip by pure chance.

What this chapter answers: how big is the noise, why doesn't averaging always help, and how do we set a bar that noise rarely crosses?

docs.title: 7.1 The intuition
docs.text:
You weigh yourself on a cheap bathroom scale. It says 71.3, then 70.8, then 71.1. Each reading wobbles, but the average of 30 readings is much steadier than any one. That's random noise, and averaging beats it.

Now imagine the floor slowly tilts during the morning. All 30 readings drift together. Averaging them doesn't remove the tilt: you get a steady, wrong number. That's correlated noise, called red noise, and averaging can't beat it.

A planet's dip lasts hours. So the question is never "how much does one reading wobble?" It's "how much does a few-hour average wobble?" Slow drifts decide that.

With JavaScript on, this spot shows a made-up light curve with a dip hidden in noise, and sliders to change the dip, the noise and the averaging.

Try it. The grey dots are measurements and the amber line is their average. Turn the noise up and the dip sinks out of sight. Average more points together and it comes back, because random wobble shrinks when you average. Now turn on the slow drift: averaging stops helping, because a drift is not random wobble. This is why our detector measures the wobble over the same length of time as the dip, and why it first removes slow drifts with a 2-day filter. The numbers here are made up for the demonstration, and this is a harsh case.

docs.title: Where the wobble comes from
docs.text:
• Photon noise. Light arrives as separate particles (photons). Counting them is like counting raindrops in a bucket: the count naturally varies by about its square root. Brighter stars give more photons, so relatively less noise.
  • The telescope. Pointing jitter, heating, thruster firings, scattered light from Earth and Moon (Lab 2's quality flags).
  • The star itself. Stars have spots, flares and boiling surfaces (granulation) that change their brightness slowly.

docs.title: White and red noise
docs.text:
White noise: each measurement's wobble is independent of the last one. Averaging N of them shrinks the wobble by √N.

Red noise: neighbouring measurements wobble together. Averaging helps much less. Real TESS data always has some, and red noise makes transit searches much harder than white-noise maths suggests LIKELY.

docs.title: Signal-to-noise ratio
docs.text: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compares the dip's depth with the wobble of an average over the dip's length. SNR 7 means the dip is 7 times bigger than a typical few-hour wobble. NASA's planet search uses a bar of 7.1 LIKELY; ours is 7.

docs.title: The look-elsewhere effect
docs.text: If you check one spot, a 7-times wobble is incredibly rare. But a search checks every time and every dip length: thousands of tries per sector. Rare things happen when you try often enough. That's why our search also runs on upside-down data (Chapter 8): it counts how many fakes noise produces with the same number of tries.

docs.title: Measuring the wobble robustly
docs.text:
The standard deviation (σ) is the usual measure of spread, but one wild point can inflate it. We use a robust version that ignores a few outliers:

σ ≈ 1.4826 × median( | x − median(x) | )

  • Take each value's distance from the middle value, then the middle of those distances (the MAD, median absolute deviation).
  • The factor 1.4826 makes it equal σ for well-behaved (bell-curve) noise.

docs.title: Averaging
docs.text:
σN = σ1 / √N

  • σ1: the wobble of one measurement. σN: the wobble of an average of N measurements.
  • Example: 2,015 ppm per 2-minute point, averaged over 1 hour (N = 30): 2,015 / √30 ≈ 368 ppm, if the noise were white.

docs.title: SNR
docs.text:
SNR = depth / σD

  • σD: the wobble of an average over the dip's duration D, measured, not computed with Eq. 7.2.
  • Our detector measures σD directly: it takes every possible D-hour average in the sector and measures their robust spread. Red noise is automatically included.

docs.title: How rare is 7σ?
docs.text: For pure bell-curve noise, the chance of one average falling 7σ below normal is about 1 in 780 billion. A sector gives our search tens of thousands of tries (thousands of ten-minute positions × 8 box lengths). Pure white noise would almost never cross the bar. Yet on upside-down TOI-1338 data, noise crossed it 6 times in 10 sectors VERIFIED. That's the strongest evidence that real TESS noise isn't white or bell-shaped: it has slow drifts and sudden jumps.

docs.title: 7.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
In pipeline/detect_v2.py:

Function What it does Why detrend() flattens slow trends with a 2-day "biweight" filter (from the wotan toolkit) removes star spots and drifts, but keeps dips up to 15 hours (Chapter 9 measured 90 to 100% kept) bin10() averages into 10-minute bins fewer, steadier points box_scores() for each length D, measures the robust spread of all D-hour averages: σD red-noise-aware SNR find_events() keeps boxes with SNR ≥ 7 the bar

A trade-off to understand: a shorter flattening window removes more red noise, but it also eats long dips. Version 1 of our detector used a 1-day window and lost real transits. Version 2 uses 2 days (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.5 Worked example: one star, four noise numbers
docs.text:
Kepler-16, sector 82, one hour of data, measured on your PC VERIFIED (and in Lab 3):

Method One-hour noise lightkurve's quick estimate (flattens with a 3.4-hour window) 229 ppm NASA's own estimate, stored in the file header ("CDPP") 542 ppm our binned scatter after a 0.25-day flatten 573 ppm our binned scatter after a 2-day flatten (what our detector sees) 908 ppm what white noise would give (Eq. 7.2) 368 ppm

Same data, a factor of 4 apart. The quick estimate flattens so hard that it removes most of the slow wobble. It even lands below the white-noise value, which is a warning sign by itself. Our own 19 October report used that quick number (236 ppm), and it fed an early claim that we could find planets of 2 to 5 Earth radii. Injection tests later measured the real floor: about 6 VERIFIED. Corrected and logged.

The lesson: a noise number means nothing without the method. Quote the one that matches how your search sees the data, and check it against the file's own CDPP.

docs.title: 7.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• We can: measure the noise our search actually faces, and set a bar whose false-alarm rate we've measured (upside-down data).
  • We can't assume bell-curve maths. 7σ is not "one in 780 billion" in real TESS data.
  • Not yet known (not tested): how much of Kepler-16's extra hour-scale noise is the stars themselves and how much is the spacecraft. Comparing quiet and noisy sectors would tell us.

docs.title: 8. Our detector: finding a dip in the noise
docs.text:
Chapter 8 · about 30 min · Maths: averages, square roots, ratios · Code: pipeline/detect_v2.py

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Slide a box along the light curve; the score peaks at the dip.sliding boxscoreSlide a box along the light curve; the score peaks at the dip.

1-minute summary

  • What: how our program scans a light curve and flags dips, with honest tests of how well it works.
  • Why: this is the heart of the hunt, and a search that finds nothing only means something if we know what it can see.
  • You will be able to: explain what the detector finds, what it misses, and why.

The story

A 2024 paper had predicted that TOI-1338 b would cross on 16 December 2025. Our detector found a dip that same night, about an hour later than predicted VERIFIED. Across all 8 sectors with a known crossing, though, it found the planet in only 4 VERIFIED. Half is an honest score, more honest than a perfect run on easy data. This chapter is about how the detector works, and about the other half it missed.

In plain words

This program scans a light curve and points at dips that might be planets. It finds the known planet TOI-1338 b in half the sectors where it crossed VERIFIED, and it catches fake planets about 6 Earth sizes and up VERIFIED.

What this chapter answers: how does our search decide "this might be a planet", and how good is it?

docs.title: 8.1 The intuition
docs.text:
You're listening for a quiet whistle in a noisy room. A single loud clap could fool you, so you don't react to one instant. Instead you ask: "is it consistently a bit different for a few seconds?" A long, steady change is easier to pick out than a single blip, even if it's quiet.

A transit is that steady change: a small dip lasting hours. Our detector averages the light over a few hours at a time and asks whether any stretch is unusually dim compared with how much stretches normally wobble.

docs.title: 8.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
The method is a matched filter with a box shape: we slide a box-shaped template of a given length along the data and measure how dim each stretch is. The key number is the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR):

SNR = (how much dimmer this stretch is) ÷ (how much stretches of this length normally vary)

An SNR of 7 means "seven times bigger than a normal wobble". We use 7 as the bar, close to NASA's 7.1 LIKELY. But a bar only means something if we measure how often noise alone crosses it. That's why we also run the search on flipped data (section 8.5).

docs.title: 8.3 The technical explanation
docs.text:
The steps, with every symbol:

  1. Mask the eclipses. The stars eclipse each other every binary period Pbin. We use the known Pbin (14.6084 days for TOI-1338) and find where in that cycle the deep eclipse falls in each sector. Data within 1.5 eclipse-lengths of either eclipse is set aside.
  2. Flatten (detrend). Stars and the spacecraft cause slow drifts. We fit a smooth curve with a moving window of 2 days (a "biweight", which ignores outliers) and divide it out. The window must be much longer than a transit, or the flattening eats the dip. v1 used 1 day, which was too short for 6-hour dips.
  3. Bin. Average the 2-minute points into 10-minute bins. When the data itself is spaced wider (30 minutes in TESS's first two years and in Kepler), each bin is one data point wide instead.
  4. Slide boxes. For each length D in 3, 4, 5, 6.5, 8, 10, 12 and 15 hours, compute the average brightness m of every D-long stretch.
  5. Score. For each length, SNR = (median − m) ÷ σD, where σD is the robust spread of all the box averages of that length (1.4826 × the median absolute deviation, a version of the standard deviation that isn't thrown off by a few odd values).
  6. Keep peaks with SNR ≥ 7 and merge overlapping ones into one event.

Why step 5 measures the spread from the box averages themselves: if the noise were purely random ("white"), averaging N points would shrink it by √N. Real data has slow wiggles ("red noise") that don't average away. Measuring the spread of real box averages includes those wiggles, so the SNR stays honest.

docs.title: 8.4 Our implementation (the code)
docs.text:
All of this is in pipeline/detect_v2.py, about 130 lines. The important functions:

Function Input Output What can go wrong load(path) a SPOC or QLP light-curve file time t, flux f, number of gaps filled (and, if asked, which column it used) missing PDCSAP data (filled from SAP); QLP needs SPOC's good stretches eclipse_mask(t, f, P, ...) data + binary period and eclipse lengths which points to keep wrong period or eclipse lengths leave eclipse edges in detrend(t, f, window_d=2.0) kept data flattened flux gaps create edge effects (Figure 8.2) box_scores(bt, bf, dur_h) 10-min bins, one length box centres, SNR, box averages too few bins → no score find_events(t, f, thr=7) kept data list of events (time, length, SNR, depth) noise bumps above 7 (false alarms)

Running python detect_v2.py runs a self-check: 27 days of pure random noise must give no event, and a hidden 6-hour, 700 ppm dip must be found at the right time. Both pass (VERIFIED, ran on 2026-10-20).

docs.title: 8.5 Worked example: TOI-1338, sector 98
docs.text:
Figure 8.1. The raw light curve. The black streaks are the stars eclipsing each other (masked before searching). The amber band is TOI-1338 b's transit on 16 Dec 2025. Data: NASA TESS via MAST. Figure 8.2. After masking and flattening (top), the 6.5-hour box score (bottom) crosses 7 only at the planet. Look at the sharp swings beside gaps (near days 4024.5 and 4038.5): edges of gaps cause fake signals, one of our known weaknesses.

The search finds the transit with SNR 9.0, depth about 2,100 ppm, about 1.1 hours after Wang and Liu's predicted time VERIFIED.

docs.title: How good is it? Three honest tests
docs.text:
1. Re-finding the known planet. TOI-1338 b crossed in 8 sectors where we have data at the right moment. v2 finds it in 4 VERIFIED. In the 4 it misses, the dip is only 3.7 to 6.5 times the noise: below our bar.

2. Fake planets. We hid computer-made transits of known sizes in sector 98 and ran the search VERIFIED:

Figure 8.3. Fake planets found, by size. v2 (amber) reaches about 6 Earth radii; neither version finds 5 or smaller in this star.

3. False alarms. Turn the light curve upside down (2 − flux). Now any real dip becomes a bump, so anything the search finds is noise or spacecraft effects. At SNR 7, v2 still finds 6 fake events in 10 sectors, some as strong as SNR 12.6 VERIFIED. That's why we can't just lower the bar.

docs.title: A fourth test: can we clean up the fakes automatically?
docs.text:
Many fake dips sit next to a data gap (where the spacecraft paused) or a momentum dump (a short thruster firing that jolts the pointing). So I tried rejecting any dip close to one. It removed 4 of the 6 fakes, but it also threw away 2 of the 4 real crossings of TOI-1338 b: one sat 0.17 days from a thruster firing, the other 0.09 days from a gap. On this star, real and fake dips sit at the same kinds of distances, so no cut-off separates them.

So the rule became gentler. Closeness to a gap or a firing is now a warning flag shown to a human, not an automatic rejection. Only a dip that also appears in the flipped data is thrown out. Result: all 4 real crossings kept, and 4 of the 6 fakes carry a warning (pipeline/veto_test.py, VERIFIED). The lesson: with one dip at a time, you can't clean this data without losing planets. You need several dips that fit one orbit.

docs.title: A fifth test: the same dip in a second, independent product
docs.text:
Half of your G1 stars only have QLP light curves (made by MIT from TESS's full-frame pictures, Chapter 3). So I ran the search on QLP's version of sector 98.

  • First try: a mess. QLP's raw light had fake dips up to 44 times the noise, and QLP's own cleaned version shrank the planet's 2,400 ppm dip to about 700 ppm (its cleaning eats long dips). The planet was missed both ways.
  • The clue: every strong fake sat inside stretches of time that NASA's SPOC pipeline throws away (scattered light that comes back at the same point in each TESS orbit). QLP keeps those stretches.
  • The fix: use QLP's flux that keeps long dips (sys_rm_flux) and keep only SPOC's good stretches. Result: one event, the planet, at SNR 10.1 and 2,275 ppm, within about 9 minutes of where SPOC put it. Fakes dropped from 9 to 2.

That's rule C8 from Chapter 10 in action: the same dip, at the same time, in two products made by different teams. VERIFIED for this one sector; borrowing SPOC's good stretches for stars that have no SPOC file is still untested.

Found later by an outside review (23 October): two holes this test could not see. Before sector 56, QLP has no sys_rm_flux, and the loader quietly took the cleaned column that eats long dips; and data spaced 30 minutes apart filled only one 10-minute bin in three, so every box failed the coverage rule and the search returned nothing, with no error. Both are fixed, with checks that hide a dip at five spacings and in our real files (pipeline/test_detect_v2_paths.py, VERIFIED). Old QLP sectors now keep their dips, but their raw light is about six times noisier than SPOC's, so they count for little. The lesson: a search that silently finds nothing looks exactly like a quiet star.

docs.title: A sixth test: fake planets that move like real ones
docs.text:
Test 2 had a weakness: its fake planets crossed on a perfect schedule, always lasting 6.4 hours. A real planet around two suns doesn't do that (Chapter 5). So I used STANLEY's own fake-planet maker, which works out each crossing with a real three-body orbit calculation. First, two bugs in STANLEY itself had to be found and worked around:

  • It checked its planned crossings against the data before adding them, and kept only the ones that already showed a dip. With no dip there yet, it kept none. So for hours it made "fake planets" with zero crossings.
  • A number was passed as a list of one item, which newer Python maths libraries refuse.

Then 6 fake planets (4, 6 and 8 Earth radii, orbits of 130 and 200 days) went into all 40 sectors of TOI-1338, giving 33 crossings that last anywhere from 6.8 to 15.3 hours VERIFIED:

Planet size Dip depth Crossings found 4 Earth radii 850 ppm 0 of 10 6 Earth radii 1,900 ppm 8 of 10 8 Earth radii 3,400 ppm 10 of 10
  • Good news: our 2-day flattening kept about 90 to 100% of every dip's depth, even the 15-hour ones. So the cleaning step isn't eating realistic, long, irregular crossings.
  • Hidden loss: 3 of the 33 crossings landed inside the binary's eclipses, which we cut out before searching. Those planets were lost before the search even looked. That's about 1 crossing in 11.
  • Same floor as before: about 6 Earth radii, now measured with realistic crossings. No false alarms appeared.

Limits (honest): only 33 crossings, one star, one orbit angle per planet, and STANLEY never makes crossings of the smaller star. A proper sensitivity map needs hundreds of fake planets.

docs.title: A seventh test: does the quality filter, or the kind of flux, matter?
docs.text:
Our search throws away every measurement NASA flags as possibly bad (the HARD filter). Two published crossings of TOI-1338 b, in sectors 30 and 62, fall where that leaves no data at all. So we asked: would a milder filter (DEFAULT) let us see them?

There was a catch, found by reading the files first: in every one of those restored stretches NASA's cleaned flux (PDCSAP) is blank, and only the raw flux (SAP) exists. So the test needed three versions, changing one thing at a time:

Arm Flux Filter Compares A0 cleaned (PDCSAP) HARD our baseline, rerun and matched exactly to the saved results A1 raw (SAP) HARD A0 vs A1: the flux alone A2 raw (SAP) DEFAULT A1 vs A2: the filter alone

The rules for reading the result were written down before anything ran (experiments/quality_mask/SPEC.md). Results, all on this one star:

  • The milder filter finds both missing crossings. In sectors 62 (a measured time) and 30 (only a prediction), an event appears within 0.3 days of the published time, at 12.1 and 10.5 times the noise VERIFIED.
  • But it costs sensitivity everywhere else. Transits that don't touch the restored data got weaker by a median of 0.5 noise units, up to 2.2. Fake 6-Earth-radius planets went from 2 found of 7 to 0 of 7, and 7-Earth-radius ones from 7 of 7 to 3 of 7 VERIFIED. Restored data is noisier and has up to 8 times the background light.
  • False alarms: undecided. In upside-down data, events containing restored data came at about 6.8 per 100 days against about 1 per 100 days without, but with so few events the ranges overlap, so the rule we set in advance was not triggered. "Not triggered" is not the same as "safe" VERIFIED.
  • A surprise about the flux, not the filter. With the same cadences, raw SAP flux found the published crossing in 7 of 8 sectors; our cleaned PDCSAP baseline found 4 VERIFIED. A follow-up check (not planned in advance, so weaker evidence) showed the transit depth is the same in both. What differs is the detector's noise estimate: in sectors 6, 34 and 37 it is 2 to 3 times larger in the cleaned flux VERIFIED. Why is not known.

What this does to earlier numbers

The "mostly the data" conclusion below was drawn from the cleaned flux only. On this star, part of the limit comes from how noisy the cleaned flux looks to our detector. Nothing is changed in the production detector: this is one star, two new crossings (one of them a prediction), and a few injections. The next steps are in RESUME.md.

docs.title: 8.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• We can conclude: the code works as designed (self-check), it finds a real planet transit when the transit is strong enough, and for a star like TOI-1338 its single-sector floor is about 6 Earth radii.
  • We can't conclude: that "nothing found" means "no planet". It means "nothing bigger than about 6 Earths crossed in this sector", and only for stars this bright or brighter.
  • The limit is partly the data. The planet's missed dips are weak in the cleaned flux, and spacecraft effects make bumps as strong as real dips. But the seventh test shows that, for the same cadences, the raw flux gave the detector a quieter noise estimate in several sectors, so "mostly the data" was too strong.
  • What came next: the gap and thruster rules became warning flags (test 4); fake planets that move like real ones were tested (test 6, and Chapter 9); and the stacked search, STANLEY, was run on TOI-1338 (Chapter 12). Smarter quality flags and a pixel tool are still to build.

Not a discovery

TOI-1338 b has been known since 2020. Everything in this chapter is a test of our tools on a known planet.
