docs.title: 9. Fake planets: injection and recovery
docs.text:
Chapter 9 · about 20 min · Maths: fractions, one square root

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Hide a fake planet, then see if the search finds it.hidden fake planetreal datafound?Hide a fake planet, then see if the search finds it.

1-minute summary

  • What: hiding fake planets of known size in real data and counting how many the search finds.
  • Why: it turns "we found nothing" into "nothing bigger than a known size crossed here".
  • You will be able to: read the result of an injection and recovery test.

The story

How small a planet could we have missed? We hid fake ones in real TOI-1338 data to find out. A planet of 6 Earth radii was found 5 times in 7, and one of 7 Earth radii every time. At 5 Earth radii and below, never VERIFIED. That is what turns 'we found nothing' into a sentence with a number in it: nothing bigger than about 6 Earth sizes crossed here.

In plain words

To know what your search can find, hide fake planets of known sizes in real data and count how many it finds. Without that, an empty result means nothing.

What this chapter answers: how do we measure a search, what makes the test honest, and what have our tests shown so far?

docs.title: 9.1 The intuition
docs.text:
A teacher wants to know whether a metal detector works on the school field. She doesn't just walk around and say "nothing beeped, so there's no metal". She buries coins of different sizes at places she's marked, walks the field, and counts which coins beeped. Now "nothing beeped" means something: no coin bigger than the smallest one it reliably finds.

Our coins are fake planets. The field is real TESS data.

docs.title: 9.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
• Injection: add a computer-made transit to the real light curve. It must go in before any cleaning, so the test includes everything that could damage a real dip.
  • Recovery: run the complete search and check whether an event appears at the right time.
  • Recovery fraction: found ÷ hidden, for each planet size. Plotted against size, it shows the search's floor: the smallest planet it finds most of the time.
  • Professionals do this. NASA's Kepler pipeline measured its own efficiency by injecting fake transits into its real pixel data LIKELY. Every claimed "no planets here" in the literature leans on a test like this.

docs.title: What makes the test honest
docs.text:
Compass (20 October) listed what a weak injection test gets wrong. Our first test had all five:

Weakness Why it matters Fixed? Fakes on a perfect timetable, all the same length real two-star crossings wander and change length (Chapter 6) yes: STANLEY-timed fakes Fakes never placed inside the eclipse mask planets lost to masking were invisible in the counts yes: now counted separately Too few trials a recovery fraction from 7 trials is very uncertain (9.3) not yet Injected into already-cleaned NASA data (PDCSAP) NASA's own cleaning isn't tested not yet One star, one sector another star's noise is different not yet

docs.title: Making a realistic dip
docs.text: A planet blocks a fraction of the star's light: about (planet radius ÷ star radius)² (Chapter 2). But a star's edge looks darker than its centre (limb darkening), so a planet crossing the middle blocks a brighter patch, and the dip's centre is deeper than that simple formula. The batman toolkit (Kreidberg 2015) draws the full shape: a curved bottom and gradual edges.

docs.title: How sure is a recovery fraction?
docs.text:
If the true recovery rate is p and you try N times, the count you get wobbles:

σp = √( p (1 − p) / N )

  • 8 found out of 10: p = 0.8, σ = √(0.8 × 0.2 / 10) = 0.13, so 80% ± 13%.
  • 1 found out of 4: 25% ± 22%. Four trials can't tell 25% from 50%.
  • For ± 3%, you need about 200 trials per size. That's why the next test is "hundreds of planets".

docs.title: Timing the fakes like real ones
docs.text: STANLEY's N-body code (Chapter 6) gives each fake planet real crossing times and lengths. Our wrapper takes those times, and STANLEY's injector adds a batman shape at each one. Getting it working took finding a bug: its injector threw away every crossing (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 9.5 Worked example: three tests, one answer
docs.text:
Test Fakes Found at 6 Earth radii Found at 4 Depth kept Timetable fakes, sector 98 VERIFIED 49 5 of 7 none not measured STANLEY-timed, 40 sectors VERIFIED 33 crossings 8 of 10 0 of 10 90 to 100% Your Lab 6, sector 98 VERIFIED 20 4 of 4 0 of 4 92 to 96%

Three different tests agree: our search reliably finds single crossings of planets about 6 Earth radii and bigger around a star like TOI-1338, and almost never smaller than 5. The 2-day cleaning keeps over 90% of a real dip's depth, even for 15-hour crossings.

And one new loss: 3 of 33 realistic crossings fell inside the stars' eclipses, so they were cut out before the search looked VERIFIED. About 1 crossing in 11 is invisible to us whatever its size.

docs.title: 9.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• We can say: "for TOI-1338-like stars, nothing bigger than about 6 Earth radii crossed in the searched data, apart from the known planet, with about 1 crossing in 11 hidden by eclipses".
  • We can't say anything about planets smaller than 5 Earth radii from single crossings. That's what stacking (STANLEY, Chapter 12) is for.
  • We can't yet give these numbers for fainter G1 stars. Each brightness level needs its own test.

docs.title: 10. Vetting

docs.title: 10. Vetting: when does a dip deserve a name?
docs.text:
Chapter 10 · about 25 min · Maths: percentages, comparing two numbers with an error bar

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Most dips do not survive the tests.dipstestscandidateMost dips do not survive the tests.

1-minute summary

  • What: the tests that try to kill a dip before anyone else has to.
  • Why: about one in four of NASA's own TESS planet candidates later turned out to be something else. VERIFIED
  • You will be able to: name the impostors and the test that catches each one.

The story

When TOI-1338 b was first found, fake dips in one sector turned out to be the spacecraft jittering just before its thrusters fired VERIFIED. We took the lesson: our detector now flags dips near those firings for a human instead of deleting them, because deleting also threw away real ones. Vetting is the habit of asking, of every dip, what else could do this.

In plain words

Finding a dip is the easy part, because most dips are not planets. Vetting is the set of tests that tries to kill a dip, and only one that survives gets a name.

What this chapter answers: how do we tell a planet's dip from all the things that imitate one?

docs.title: 10.1 The intuition
docs.text: A detective with a suspect doesn't ask "could they have done it?" They ask "what else could explain this?" and rule each explanation out. Vetting works the same way. For every dip we list the usual impostors and run a test that each one would fail.

docs.title: 10.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
Vetting means testing a signal against every known false positive: something that isn't a planet but makes a planet-like dip. The scale of the problem: of 2,241 TESS planet candidates from the first two years, 565 (about 25%) were later flagged as false positives VERIFIED. And those had already passed NASA's own checks.

The usual impostors:

Impostor How it fakes a dip The test that catches it Our own binary's eclipses leftover bits after masking does the dip repeat at the same point in the binary's orbit? A different binary in the same pixels TESS pixels are huge (~21 arcseconds), so a faint eclipsing pair nearby blends in does the light's centre shift during the dip? (centroid test) The spacecraft thruster firings (momentum dumps) make the pointing wobble is the dip next to a dump or a flagged cadence? Scattered light, asteroids background changes or a rock crossing the pixels per-pixel and background checks The star itself spots, pulsations, flares does a transit shape beat a wave, a step or a line? Our own software bad detrending carves a dip does it survive many different detrendings?

docs.title: NASA's bar and ours
docs.text:
NASA's SPOC pipeline flags a candidate at MES > 7.1 with at least 2 transits; QLP uses SNR > 9; a centroid shift of 1 pixel or more points to a background binary VERIFIED. The Warwick circumbinary team kept an event only if it survived at least 18 of 21 different detrendings and a transit model beat a sinusoid, a step and a straight line VERIFIED.

Our own bar is stricter on purpose. A clean record is how an independent citizen scientist earns trust. The rules for a single circumbinary dip (C1 to C11, from the wave 4 research):

Rule Test Pass means C1 strength SNR ≥ 7 (Chapter 8) C2 robustness found in at least 18 of 21 detrendings C3 shape a transit model beats sine, step and line C4 duration under 1 day, and possible for an orbit outside the stability limit (Chapter 4) C5 not an eclipse not at a binary phase shared by 3 or more events C6 not a neighbour no centroid shift, no correlated dip in nearby pixels C7 not the spacecraft no flagged data in the dip; not just before a momentum dump unless pixel checks clear it C8 independent data seen in at least 2 different light-curve products C9 physical size implied radius under 2 Jupiters whichever star it crosses C10 smoking gun if 2+ dips: timing and duration fit a circumbinary orbit C11 two keys Claude's analysis passes and you agree

docs.title: The circumbinary smoking gun
docs.text: One test is special to our quest. A real planet orbiting two stars crosses them while they move. Its transits are shorter near the binary's primary-eclipse phase and longer near the other VERIFIED, and they come at irregular times a three-body model can predict. No fake has that fingerprint. Two dips that fit it are worth more than ten that don't.

docs.title: 10.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
Today's pipeline covers C1 (find_events in pipeline/detect_v2.py), part of C5 (the eclipse mask), part of C7 (the warning flags from veto, Chapter 8) and C4's orbit range (pipeline/stability.py). The rest is research, not code yet:

  • C2 (21 detrendings), C3 (model comparison), C6 (pixel checks), C8 (second product), C9 (size for both stars), C10 (orbit fit): not tested in code.
  • The planned output is a one-page vetting sheet per event, readable on your phone, with every rule as a pass/fail line.

We ran C6 by hand once, on the TOI-1338 dip of 16 December 2025: the dimming came from the target's own pixels and the light's centre didn't move (0.0 to 0.2σ). That is a manual check, recorded in research/wave-3-pipeline/.

docs.title: 10.5 Worked example: how TOI-1338 b fooled people for a moment
docs.text:
When TOI-1338 b was being confirmed, some dips in sector 3 looked like transits. They were traced to pointing jitter just before momentum dumps, a spacecraft effect, not the planet VERIFIED. The team found this with pixel-level (PSF) analysis.

That's exactly why rule C7 exists, and why our own veto test (Chapter 8) found fakes clustered near gaps and dumps. The lesson: even professionals meet fakes, and the way out is a specific test for each impostor, not a gut feeling.

docs.title: Worked example 2: the same impostor in our own data
docs.text:
On 20 October 2026 our pipeline ran on Kepler-16 (a real G1 binary) and flagged one dip in sector 54: about 0.2% deep, 15 hours, SNR 7.8. Treated like a real candidate:

  • C5 (not an eclipse): the real primary eclipse was at BTJD 2771.73, 13% deep, exactly where the catalogue said; the dip was 4 days later. Pass.
  • C7 (not the spacecraft): a momentum dump at BTJD 2776.07, 0.41 days after the dip, with quality flags set around it. Fail. This is pointing jitter before a dump, the same impostor as in the TOI-1338 b story.
  • C8 (second product): QLP shows nothing there. Fail.

Verdict: impostor. The lesson for us: the rule was right, but our code checked "within 0.25 days either side" instead of the rule's "up to 0.5 days before". The code now follows the rule. Writing the rule down first, then checking the code against it, is how this got caught.

docs.title: 10.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• Passing vetting does not make a planet. It makes a candidate: a dip with no known innocent explanation. Confirmation needs more data, usually from other telescopes.
  • Failing one test doesn't always kill a dip. Some rules are flags for a closer look (C7 near a dump, for example). Others are hard stops (C9: a "planet" bigger than 2 Jupiters is a star).
  • The path after vetting changed in 2026. NASA's community candidate site (ExoFOP) now accepts candidates only after they're published, in a peer-reviewed journal or a research note citing a published method VERIFIED. So our order is: vetting, two keys, write-up, then upload. That decision is still yours (it's in the decision log).

docs.title: 11. Pixels and neighbours: is the dip on our star?
docs.text:
Chapter 11 · about 20 min · Maths: weighted averages, fractions

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Whose light dimmed? Look at the pixels.neighbourour starWhose light dimmed? Look at the pixels.

1-minute summary

  • What: checking the pixels to see whether a dip sits on our star or on a faint neighbour.
  • Why: TESS pixels are big, so several stars share them.
  • You will be able to: say what "the centre of light moved" means and why it matters.

The story

On 16 December 2025 TOI-1338 b crossed, and the pixel test asked whose light had dimmed. The dimming sat on the target's own pixels, and the centre of light moved by 0.001 arcseconds, a tenth of the chance wobble VERIFIED. One TESS pixel spans about 21 arcseconds LIKELY, so neighbours crowd in, and eight catalogued stars share this 11 by 11 patch. The test says the dip belongs to our star.

In plain words

TESS's pixels are big, so a dip in our star's light curve could really come from a faint neighbour. We look at the pixels themselves to see where the dimming sits.

What this chapter answers: how can a neighbour fake a planet, how do we tell, and what did TOI-1338's pixels say?

docs.title: 11.1 The intuition
docs.text: A street has three lamps close together, and you're measuring their combined glow from far away. The glow dips. Which lamp flickered? Take a photo during the dip and one before, subtract them, and the flickering lamp is the only one that shows up in the difference. Or watch the centre of the glow: if the left lamp dims, the glow's centre shifts right.

docs.title: 11.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
• Big pixels. One TESS pixel is 21 arcseconds LIKELY. Kepler-16 has 15 catalogued stars within 1 arcminute, 4 of them bright enough to matter VERIFIED. TOI-1338's 11 × 11 pixel stamp holds 8 stars brighter than magnitude 16 VERIFIED.
  • Blends. A neighbour 5 magnitudes fainter gives 1% of the light. If it's an eclipsing binary dipping by 20%, our light curve dips by 0.2%: exactly a planet-sized dip. This is one of the commonest impostors (Chapter 10, rule C6).
  • Dilution. Even when the dip is on our star, neighbours' light makes it look shallower, so the planet looks smaller. SPOC estimates the share of light that's really from the target (CROWDSAP): 0.89 for Kepler-16, 0.99 for TOI-1338 VERIFIED. Cleaned PDCSAP light curves are corrected for this; raw SAP ones aren't.
  • How professionals check. Kepler's validation stage used difference images and centroid offsets for every candidate LIKELY. A centroid shift is a warning sign, not a verdict: it has to be compared with the shift you'd expect if the dip were on target.

docs.title: Dilution
docs.text:
observed depth = true depth × ftarget

  • ftarget: the target's share of the light in the aperture.
  • Kepler-16 (f = 0.89): a true 1,000 ppm dip shows as 890 ppm. Ignore that, and the planet's size comes out √0.89 = 0.94 times too small.

docs.title: The centre of the light (centroid)
docs.text:
x̄ = Σ xi Fi / Σ Fi

  • Each pixel's position xi weighted by its light Fi: the balance point of the light.

docs.title: What shift to expect
docs.text:
Think of just two sources: our target (share ft) and the neighbours lumped together (share fo), a distance d apart. Working through Eq. 11.2 for a small dip of depth δ (our own rough calculation):

dip on target: Δx̄ ≈ δ × ft × fo × d · dip on a neighbour: Δx̄ ≈ δ × ft × d

  • If the target dims, the centre moves slightly away from it, toward the neighbours, by a tiny amount (fo is small).
  • If the neighbour dims, the centre moves toward the target, about 1 ÷ fo times more. That difference is the whole test.

docs.title: An honest error bar
docs.text: The light centre wobbles all the time: pointing jitter, slow drifts. Dividing the scatter by √N assumes white noise (Chapter 7) and makes a shift look more significant than it is. Compass found that mistake in our first pixel script. The better way: slide a window of the same length over quiet stretches, measure the shift each time, and take the spread of those chance shifts as the error.

docs.title: 11.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
Where What Status research/wave-3-pipeline/toi1338_pixel_check.py first manual check: difference image + centroid shift error bar assumed white noise labs/lab7_pixels.py difference image, centroid shift with chance-spread error, neighbours from the TIC placed on the pixels with the file's sky map (WCS) VERIFIED on TOI-1338 automated pixel tool for G1 survivors, with the expected-shift model of Eq. 11.3 Compass priority 3 not tested (not built)

Pixel files are about 50 MB per sector VERIFIED, so we only fetch them for events that survive the earlier checks.

docs.title: 11.5 Worked example: TOI-1338's crossing on 16 December 2025
docs.text:
From Lab 7, run on your PC VERIFIED:

TOI-1338, sector 98. Left: normal light. Right: dimming during the crossing. White: SPOC's aperture. Red circles: catalogued stars.
  • The dimming sits on the target's own pixels (row 4, columns 4 to 5). The bright neighbour at upper left (12.8 mag, 103″ away) shows none.
  • Centre shift: +0.001″ in row, 0.000″ in column. Chance spread from 128 quiet windows: 0.006″ and 0.012″. So the shift is 0.1 and 0.0 times the chance spread: no shift.
  • Expected (Eq. 11.3) with δ = 0.002, fo ≈ 0.01, d ≈ 60″: on target, about 0.001″; on a neighbour 60″ away, about 0.12″, which would be 10 to 20 times the chance spread and obvious.
  • Verdict: consistent with the dip being on TOI-1338, as expected for a known planet. A neighbour within a few arcseconds couldn't be ruled out this way; that needs sharper images from other telescopes.

docs.title: 11.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• We can: rule out neighbours far enough away to shift the centre measurably, using an honest error bar.
  • We can't: rule out a faint star almost exactly behind ours. Professionals use high-resolution imaging for that, which we can't do from TESS data.
  • Not built yet: the automated version for G1, and the expected-shift model in code (Compass priority 3).

docs.title: 12. STANLEY: the professionals' tool
docs.text:
Chapter 12 · about 20 min · Maths: square roots, a grid of guesses

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Try thousands of orbits and keep the one that stacks.thousands of orbits tried, the best one keptTry thousands of orbits and keep the one that stacks.

1-minute summary

  • What: STANLEY, a professionals' tool that guesses a whole orbit and adds up the light at every predicted crossing.
  • Why: crossings that wander cannot be stacked on a timetable, but predicted ones can.
  • You will be able to: read STANLEY's output and say what it did on TOI-1338.

The story

We asked STANLEY to try 20,482 possible orbits for TOI-1338, which took 33 minutes. Its best answer was 96.11 days, and the real planet takes 95.2 VERIFIED VERIFIED. Close, but 28% of all the orbits scored above 5 sigma, so the score scale cannot be trusted yet. We first misread the answer as 93.8 days, and a lab caught it.

In plain words

Each crossing of a small two-star planet is too faint to see alone, and they do not arrive on a timetable. STANLEY guesses a whole orbit, predicts every crossing, and adds up the light at those moments.

What this chapter answers: what is STANLEY, why does it need a real orbit calculation, what did it say about TOI-1338 on your PC, and why don't we trust its scores yet?

docs.title: 12.1 The intuition
docs.text:
You're listening for a faint drummer in a noisy room. Each beat is too quiet to hear. If the drummer kept perfect time, you could add up the sound at every beat and the rhythm would appear. That's how normal planet searches work: they stack dips that repeat on a timetable.

Our drummer doesn't keep time: the beats come early and late, some long, some short (Chapter 6). But if you knew the drummer's pattern, you could still add the sound at exactly the right moments. STANLEY tries thousands of possible patterns and checks which one makes the rhythm appear.

docs.title: 12.2 The scientific meaning
docs.text:
• The problem. No two-star planet smaller than 3 Earth radii had been found, though such planets make up over 75% of discoveries around single stars. They're not necessarily rare: they're hard to find, because their timing shifts are bigger than their crossings are long LIKELY.
  • The idea. For each guessed orbit (period, starting position, and optionally eccentricity), run an N-body simulation (Chapter 6), get every predicted crossing time and length, and stack the light curve at those moments.
  • The authors. David Martin and Daniel Fabrycky described STANLEY in 2021. Run on Kepler's two-star systems, it found every known planet, including all three of Kepler-47's, and showed planets under 3 Earth radii could have been found in half of them LIKELY. The software is published under the MIT licence by Martin's group at Tufts University; version 0.2.8 is installed on your PC.
  • The three stages.
    1. Detrending: fits the binary, removes the eclipses, flattens the light curve.
    2. Search: the grid of guessed orbits, each given a score in σ.
    3. Analysis: reads the grid, ranks the best orbits, and checks them.

docs.title: Why stacking helps
docs.text: If each of N crossings has SNR s on its own, and the noise is white, the stack has SNR ≈ s × √N. Four crossings of SNR 3 make an SNR-6 stack; nine make 9. That's how STANLEY reaches planets our one-dip-at-a-time search can't.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text:
Every guess is an orbit. Our TOI-1338 run tried VERIFIED:

Setting Values Planet period 173 steps from 90.05 to 100.03 days Starting angle (where on its orbit the planet starts) up to 123 steps around the full circle Eccentricity 0 only (circular): a quick test Total 20,482 orbits, in 33 minutes

A full search would add eccentricities and orientations, and many more periods. Grids grow fast: that's the price of not knowing the orbit.

docs.title: Scores and the look-elsewhere problem
docs.text: Each orbit gets a score in σ: how much darker the stacked crossings are than normal, compared with the noise. But with 20,482 tries, high scores happen by chance (Chapter 7). On your PC, the typical score was 4.2σ and 28% of all orbits scored above 5σ VERIFIED. So here "5σ" doesn't mean "rare". The scale must be calibrated: run the same grid on data with no planet (flipped, or shuffled), see how high pure noise scores, and set the bar above that.

docs.title: 12.4 Our implementation
docs.text:
STANLEY needed six fixes to run on your PC. Each one is in our wrapper scripts, not in STANLEY's own code:

Problem Fix Where Python 3.12 dropped a module (distutils) that batman needs installed setuptools STANLEY's environment It downloaded data to C: wrapper forces the cache to D: before anything downloads pipeline/stanley/run_detrend.py np.product removed in newer numpy one-line stand-in run_search.py The fake-planet maker used a 1-second time limit raised to 600 s inject_cbp.py The fake-planet maker kept only crossings that already showed a dip, so it injected zero take crossing times straight from the N-body step inject_cbp.py A one-item list passed where a number is needed return a plain number inject_cbp.py

The last two were found by calling STANLEY's pieces one at a time (field note, 20 October).

docs.title: 12.5 Worked example: STANLEY on TOI-1338
docs.text:
From Lab 8, run on your PC VERIFIED:

STANLEY's search of TOI-1338 (40 sectors, circular orbits). Left: the best score at each trial period; red dashed line: the real planet's 95.2 days LIKELY. Right: every orbit's score.
  • The peak: 18.4σ at 96.11 days, the next-best 16.3σ at 96.16 days. The real planet's period is 95.2 days.
  • Why not exactly 95.2? Our grid only tried circular orbits (the real one has e ≈ 0.09, Kostov et al. 2020), and STANLEY's own fit gave the stars slightly different masses (1.2 and 0.325 Suns, against the published 1.1 and 0.3). A slightly wrong model shifts the best guess.
  • The histogram: most orbits score 2 to 8σ just from noise and leftover wiggles. 18.4σ is far out on its own, which is encouraging. But until the scale is calibrated, it's a pointer, not a result.

Corrected, 20 October 2026

Our overnight report first said the peak was at 93.8 days. The search log prints the period range from high to low, but the results file runs low to high. Lab 8 now reads the periods from STANLEY's saved grid file and checks that its row lengths match. Logged in the mistakes register.

docs.title: 12.6 What this lets us conclude, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
• We can: run STANLEY on your PC, and it points close to the real planet's period with a strong score.
  • We can't yet: say how significant 18.4σ is (no calibration), or claim a "recovery" (circular grid, uncalibrated): still uncertain.
  • Not done yet (not tested): STANLEY's analysis stage, a calibrated run, and any G1 star.
  • Where it fits: our fast detector screens all 549 G1 stars for single strong dips; STANLEY is the slow, deep search for small planets on the most promising binaries.

  • Why: so you can find anything yourself.
  • You will be able to: find where a decision, a mistake or a result is recorded.

The story

On 19 October this project was a plan. By 21 October it had registers for decisions, mistakes, predictions and facts, because a project this young forgets fast, and Claude forgets faster. Everything in this chapter exists for one reason: so that you, or a fresh session a week from now, can pick the work up and know exactly where things stand.

In plain words

Everything we do lives in one folder on your D: drive, with a public copy on GitHub. This chapter is the map of what is where and the rules that keep it safe.

What this chapter answers: where is everything, and how does a day of work turn into a page you can read?

docs.title: 13.3 How a working day flows
docs.text:
1. An idea or a request (yours, or from a review).
  2. Compass, if it's big: what exists already, what's wrong with the idea, what to do first. Verdict before building.
  3. Build and test. Code gets a self-check; results are measured, not eyeballed.
  4. Record. Results into a report; facts into the claims register with labels; decisions and mistakes into their registers.
  5. Teach. A field note, the same day (your rule of 20 October). Bigger new ideas get a chapter section.
  6. Publish. Commit to git, push to GitHub, rebuild this site. The guard script book/tools/teach_check.py prints "Book is N commits behind" during publishing; it should say 0.

docs.title: 13.4 Git and GitHub in five sentences
docs.text: Git keeps every saved version of every file. A commit is one saved snapshot with a message saying what changed and why. Pushing copies commits to GitHub, where the project is public at github.com/M1Smacker/second-sun. Because every change is a commit, nothing is ever truly lost, and anyone can check what we did and when. This book is built from the committed files only, in a fresh copy, so what you read is exactly what's saved.

docs.title: 14. Credit and publishing
docs.text:
What this chapter answers: once we find something, how does it become a recognised discovery with your name on it?

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Publish first, then NASA's candidate site.a dipvettingshort paperExoFOPpublish first, then NASA's candidate sitePublish first, then NASA's candidate site.

1-minute summary

  • What: the order of steps from a dip to a credited result, and what journals say about AI.
  • Why: in 2026 NASA's candidate site started wanting the write-up published first. VERIFIED
  • You will be able to: describe the steps from a dip to credit.

The story

In 2026 NASA's candidate site paused uploads on 31 March and reopened them on 19 August with a new rule: write it up and publish first VERIFIED. So a find of ours would not start with a click on submit. It would start with a short paper, and two keys turned: yours and mine. This chapter is the map from a dip to a name with your name beside it.

In plain words

A dip does not become ours when we see it. It becomes ours when it is written up and published, and then shared with the TESS team.

You need first: L6 Two-key vetting (outline).

docs.title: The order of steps
docs.text:
1. Two keys: my analysis and your own check both pass.
  2. Write-up: a short note in RNAAS (free), or a full paper with a professional team.
  3. ExoFOP: only a published candidate can be uploaded, and uploading needs approval VERIFIED. This rule arrived on 19 August 2026, after a pause that started on 31 March VERIFIED.
  4. TESS team: they decide whether it becomes a TOI.

docs.title: Journals and AI
docs.text:
• MNRAS: AI can't be an author, and how we used it (including code and data processing) goes in the cover letter and in the paper VERIFIED. You can submit without a university VERIFIED.
  • A&A: AI can't be an author; help with language, coding and searching needs no disclosure if a person oversees it LIKELY.

docs.title: What this means for our hunt
docs.text: Plan the write-up as part of vetting, not after it. The first candidate's timeline is: two keys, RNAAS draft, publication, then ExoFOP.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Does citing published tools we use count as "a previously published method" for an RNAAS route? Only ExoFOP support can say.

docs.title: 15. Our mistakes, as lessons
docs.text:
Chapter 15 · about 15 min · no maths

ListenPauseStopSpeed SlowNormalFastUses the voice on your own device. Five patterns behind fifteen mistakes.numberspattern 1automationpattern 2recordpattern 3rulespattern 4wordspattern 5Five patterns behind fifteen mistakes.

1-minute summary

  • What: fifteen logged mistakes, five patterns, and the rule each one left behind.
  • Why: the patterns are how careful people still get things wrong, anywhere.
  • You will be able to: spot the five patterns in your own work.

The story

Kepler-16's noise, by one quick method, is about 229 ppm. NASA's own number in the file header says 542, and what our detector really sees after cleaning is 908 VERIFIED. We had quoted the small one. A lab caught it, because a lab has to print real numbers from real data. Every mistake in this chapter is that kind of mistake: small, plausible and invisible until you check.

In plain words

In the first two days we logged 15 mistakes. None reached anyone outside the project, and each one left a rule behind.

What this chapter answers: what went wrong, why, and what each mistake taught us. The full list, with dates and costs, is in research/mistakes.md.

docs.title: Lesson 1: check numbers against the data, not against your expectations
docs.text:
What happened The rule it left An early estimate said we could find planets of 2 to 5 Earth radii. Fake-planet tests showed about 6 Every "we can see down to X" must come from an injection test (Chapter 9) Kepler-16's one-hour noise was quoted as 236 ppm. Measured the way our search sees the data, it's about 900 VERIFIED Measure noise like the detector does; compare with the file's own estimate (Chapter 7) STANLEY's best orbit was reported at 93.8 days; it's 96.1 VERIFIED Read an array's order from the data file, not a log message (Lab 8) The G1 rule "morph < 0.5" also let in 136 stars with morph = −1, meaning "not measured" VERIFIED Handle missing-value codes on purpose in every selection rule

The pattern: each number looked reasonable, so nobody checked it with a tool that could say "no". Three of these four were caught while writing this book's labs, because a lab has to show real output. Teaching is a form of testing.

docs.title: Lesson 2: test automation before trusting it
docs.text:
What happened The rule it left Timed helper sessions froze about 10 seconds in, on a permission prompt Run one tiny end-to-end test of any unattended setup while someone can still step in A fix for Avast's certificate checks broke Python's installer; 6 installs failed After any change that affects every Python start, test the installer immediately STANLEY was about to download data to the full C: drive Before running someone else's tool, search its code for where it saves files

The pattern: something that works by hand can fail when nobody is watching. Find out while someone is.

docs.title: Lesson 3: keep the record clean
docs.text: What happened The rule it left A 1.2 GB tool folder nearly went into git Ignore every .venv* folder; look at git status before adding A generated website folder (2.8 MB) was committed Ignore every site/ folder; add named paths, not whole trees The facts register claims.csv was silently ignored by git, so the book couldn't be rebuilt from GitHub Check a fresh copy builds; the publish script now does this every time Finish times were written from estimates, not the clock Read the clock (date -u) before writing any time

docs.title: Lesson 4: the code must match the written rule
docs.text: What happened The rule it left Rule C7 says "flag dips up to half a day before a thruster firing". The code checked a quarter day either side. Our first G1 dip, on Kepler-16, sat 0.41 days before a firing and slipped through When a rule is written in words, test the code against an example that sits right at its edge

docs.title: Lesson 5: communicate so you can actually decide
docs.text: What happened The rule it left The project's future story was framed as "Kuwaiti discovers a planet". You're Pakistani, living in Kuwait Never assume identity from location. Credit line: Ahmed Hanzala, independent citizen scientist (Pakistan), based in Kuwait You were asked to approve "the blueprint with my 3 additions" before the additions were written out Write out everything being approved before asking An overnight session ended on a question box and nothing ran until morning Overnight work states its defaults and keeps going; questions wait in the report

docs.title: What the mistakes have in common
docs.text:
• None was hidden. Each was logged the day it was found, with its cost, and corrected where it appeared (the book included).
  • Most were caught by a check that could disagree: a lab's real output, a fresh-copy build, a test at the edge of a rule.
  • Each left a rule, and the rules are why the next mistake is a different one.

Records · one lesson per working day

In plain words

After every working session, what we did goes here as a short lesson, the same day. If you've been away, read the notes since your last visit, newest at the bottom of the list. This is the rule from 20 October: nothing we do stays only in the chat.

Each note has the same parts: in plain words · what we did and why · the idea behind it (with links to the chapters) · how you could do it yourself · what we found, and what we didn't · one or two questions.

Date Main lesson 19 October 2026 How a research project starts: what's known, where the gap is, and measuring before deciding 20 October 2026 Testing honestly: fake planets, false alarms, a bug in a professional tool, and Compass 21 October 2026 A progress bar that has to prove itself: evidence, auto-counting and logged changes 23 October 2026 Rebuilding the book around a map: orientation, optional labs and a real-sky home page

docs.title: 19 October 2026: how a research project starts
docs.text:
Field note · day 1 · about 8 min

In plain words

We didn't touch a single light curve until we knew three things: what's already been found, where nobody has looked, and whether the data is good enough to look there. That took the whole day, and it decided our first campaign: G1, Kepler's two-star systems re-watched by TESS.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. Set the rules first. 25 rounds of questions fixed what we hunt, how sure we must be before calling something a candidate, and which decisions are yours. Rules made before the data can't be bent to fit the data.
  2. Census of what's known. Only 14 transiting two-star planets are known: 12 from Kepler and 2 from TESS VERIFIED. That's a tiny club, so even one new member would matter.
  3. Gap check. Where hasn't anyone looked? Normal planet searches look for dips that repeat on a timetable. Two-star planets break the timetable (Chapter 5), so they're under-searched in TESS data.
  4. Measured the data before choosing. I downloaded real files and measured their size VERIFIED and their noise. A quick estimate said one hour of Kepler-16's data wobbles by only 236 parts per million VERIFIED. Corrected on 20 October: that quick method was too optimistic; measured the way our search sees the data it's about 900 ppm VERIFIED (Chapter 7). The decision still stood, because the injection test measured what we can actually find.
  5. Chose G1. Kepler found thousands of eclipsing binaries LIKELY. Two-star planets' orbits slowly tilt ("precess"), so their transits switch on and off over years LIKELY. A planet that was "off" during Kepler could be "on" now in TESS. You approved it from your phone.
  6. Founded this book, with your rule: professional, clean, not gamey.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
• A research gap is a question nobody has answered with the data that exists. Ours: has anyone searched TESS data of Kepler's binaries for single, irregular transits? The census and the reading said: not systematically.
  • Measure, don't guess. "Is TESS good enough?" was answered with a number from a real file, not an opinion. You'll see this rule all through the book.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• The census: NASA's Exoplanet Archive lets anyone list known planets. We asked for every planet flagged as orbiting two stars.
  • The noise: in Lab 2 you download the same kind of file. Chapter 7 shows how to measure its noise.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Found: a clear campaign (G1), a measured data budget, and a list of rivals to watch.
  • Not yet: any searching. Day 1 was all preparation, on purpose.
  • One thing went wrong: timed helper sessions froze on a permission prompt about 10 seconds after starting, so the research continued in the main session. Lesson: test automation before trusting it overnight.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why decide the rules before looking at any data?

So the data can't bend them. If you set the bar after seeing a signal, it's too easy to set it just below that signal.

2. Why might a planet missed by Kepler be visible to TESS?

Its orbit slowly tilts (precesses). Transits switch on and off over years, so it may have been "off" during Kepler (2009 to 2013) and "on" since.

docs.title: 20 October 2026: testing honestly
docs.text:
Field note · night 1 and morning · about 12 min

In plain words

Overnight we built a better planet search and then spent most of our effort trying to break it: hiding fake planets to see which it finds, flipping the data upside down to count false alarms, and running it on a real G1 star. In the morning, a bug in the professionals' tool (STANLEY) was found and worked around, and we measured our search with fake planets that move like real ones. No new planet. But we now know what our search can and can't see.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. Detector version 2. It slides a box of 3 to 15 hours along the light curve and asks "is it darker in here than usual?" (Chapter 8). It re-found TOI-1338 b in 4 of 8 sectors VERIFIED.
  2. Fake planets. We added made-up transits of known sizes and checked which were found: down to about 6 Earth radii VERIFIED.
  3. Upside-down data. Flip the light curve (2 − brightness) and any dip becomes a bump. Whatever the search still "finds" must be noise: 6 fakes in 10 sectors VERIFIED.
  4. A failed clean-up. Throwing out dips near spacecraft events removed fakes but also half the real crossings. So those became warning flags for a human (Chapter 10).
  5. A timing check. A 2024 paper predicted a TOI-1338 b crossing on 16 December 2025. We found it VERIFIED, 56 ± 5 minutes after the predicted time.
  6. G1 frozen, QLP fixed, auto eclipse finder, Kepler-16 dry run. The one dip on Kepler-16 was the telescope wobbling before a thruster firing. Nothing survived.
  7. STANLEY installed and run (Chapter 12). Its strongest signal was near 96 days (first misread as 94; corrected in the afternoon), close to the real planet's 95.2, but its scores aren't calibrated yet.
  8. Compass reviewed our upgrade plans: REVISE. Its three points: use STANLEY's fake-planet maker instead of building one; odd and even depths only mean something for planets that repeat; centroid checks must predict the expected shift.
  9. The STANLEY bug. Its fake-planet maker placed zero transits. Cause: before adding the transits it ran them through its search scorer, which keeps only transits already showing a dip. Before injection there's no dip, so it kept none. Our wrapper now takes the transit times straight from its orbit simulation.
  10. The realistic test. 6 fake planets, 33 crossings lasting 6.8 to 15.3 hours VERIFIED. Our cleaning kept 90 to 100% of each dip. 6 Earth radii: 8 of 10 found. 8: 10 of 10. 4: none. 3 of 33 crossings were lost inside the stars' eclipses before the search even looked.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Injection and recovery is how you measure a search: add signals you know, see what comes back. It turns "we found nothing" into "nothing bigger than X crossed". Without it, a null result means nothing. Chapter 9 is all about it.

Debugging by stepping through: the STANLEY bug was found by calling its pieces one at a time. Did the orbit calculation give transit times? Yes, 13 to 29. Did they survive the next step? No. The fault sat between those two calls.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Lab 4 runs our box search on TOI-1338.
  • Lab 6 hides fake planets of several sizes and asks the search to find them.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Found: the search's floor (about 6 Earth radii), a 9% hidden loss inside eclipses, two STANLEY bugs, and a prediction confirmed.
  • Didn't: any new planet. G1 hasn't been searched yet, apart from Kepler-16.
  • Mistakes, logged: the first strict clean-up rule; a rule (C7) coded differently from how it was written; a cache that nearly wrote to C:; estimated timestamps written instead of checked ones.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why flip the light curve upside down?

A real dip becomes a bump, so the search can't find real planets in flipped data. Anything it finds there shows how often noise alone fools it.

2. 3 of 33 fake crossings fell inside eclipses. What does that mean for G1?

Even a perfect search misses about 1 crossing in 11, because we cut out the stars' eclipses before searching. Our "nothing found" results must count that loss.

docs.title: Afternoon: the Bible Overhaul begins
docs.text:
You paused the hunt so the book could catch up. Two lessons came out of the overhaul itself:

  • Labs are real runs. Every command in Labs 0 to 4 was run on your PC before it went in the book, and the "what you should see" boxes are pasted output.
  • Writing a lab caught a mistake. Our 19 October noise number for Kepler-16 (236 ppm per hour) came from a quick method that flattens away slow wobble. Measured the way our search sees the data, it's about 900 ppm; NASA's own file says 542 VERIFIED. Same data, a factor of 4 apart, depending on the method. Chapter 7 teaches why. It's logged in the mistakes register, and it probably explains the early "2 to 5 Earth radii" overstatement.
3. Why did one star's one-hour noise come out anywhere from 229 to 908 ppm?

Each method flattens the light curve differently first. The harder you flatten, the more slow wobble you remove, and the smaller the noise looks. Quote the number that matches how your search treats the data.

Later, batch 3 of the overhaul: writing Lab 8 caught a second slip. STANLEY's strongest orbit is at 96.1 days, not the 93.8 reported overnight. The search log prints the period range high to low, but the results file runs low to high. The real planet's period is 95.2 days, so the conclusion ("close") survives, but the number was wrong for half a day. Lesson: read an array's order from the data file, and check one known feature lines up. Chapter 12 and Chapter 6 are new.

Batch 4: Chapter 9 (fake planets) and Chapter 11 (pixels and neighbours), with Labs 6 and 7. Two things worth knowing: three different fake-planet tests now agree on a floor of about 6 Earth radii VERIFIED; and TOI-1338's pixels show the 16 December dip on the right star, with the light's centre steady to about a thousandth of an arcsecond VERIFIED. The pixel lab uses a better error bar than our first pixel script (Compass's point): the chance spread of the same measurement at quiet times.

Batch 5: Chapter 13 (a tour of the project), Chapter 15 (our 15 mistakes, as five lessons), Lab 9 (the whole route on a G1 star of your choice), a rebuilt learning track and a reading list. Writing Lab 9 found a real problem in the G1 list: our rule "morph < 0.5" also lets in stars whose shape was never measured (morph = −1): 136 of 552 rows VERIFIED. The first star I tried was one of them, and it showed no eclipse at all. Not fixed (the hunt is paused); it's a decision for you in the decision log, explained in Chapter 1.

Batch 6, the stress test (overhaul complete): every one of the 10 lab scripts was run again from scratch and reproduced its page's "what you should see" output exactly. The built site: 40 pages, 3,743 internal links and anchors checked, 0 broken; no long dashes in visible text; no sideways scrolling on any page at phone width (375 px) or desktop width; all 11 lab and chapter pictures load; all 39 pages are in the offline cache; the "Next" links lead through all 25 chapters and labs in one line, with no loops. Your progress page now shows TOI-1338 b's recovery (19 October) and this overhaul as milestones.

docs.title: Evening: the quality-filter experiment (you approved it, I ran it)
docs.text:
In plain words

Our search throws away data that NASA flags as possibly bad. Two known crossings of TOI-1338 b fall in thrown-away data, so we couldn't see them. I tested whether keeping that data helps. The honest answer: it finds those two crossings, but it makes the search worse everywhere else, and it might add false alarms. Separately, the test turned up a surprise about which flux the search reads.

What we did and why. First I read the files (no experiment yet) and found the catch: in every piece of restored data, NASA's cleaned flux (PDCSAP) is blank; only the raw flux (SAP) exists. So "same flux, looser filter" was impossible. I wrote the plan down before running anything (experiments/quality_mask/SPEC.md): three versions, changing one thing at a time (cleaned + strict filter = our baseline; raw + strict; raw + milder). I rebuilt the baseline from scratch and checked it matched our saved results exactly. Only then did I run the other two.

The idea behind it (Chapter 8, seventh test): change one thing at a time, and decide how you'll read the result before you see it, so you can't talk yourself into the answer you like. This is called pre-registration.

What we found (one star, so treat it as a hint): - The milder filter finds both missing crossings, sectors 62 and 30, at about 12 and 10 times the noise VERIFIED. - It lowers the strength of transits elsewhere and hurts fake-planet recovery VERIFIED; false alarms: undecided VERIFIED. - Surprise: raw flux alone, with the same data points, found the published crossing in 7 sectors of 8; the cleaned flux found 4 VERIFIED. The transits are equally deep in both. What differs is the detector's noise estimate, 2 to 3 times larger in the cleaned flux in some sectors VERIFIED. We don't know why.

What we didn't find: whether any of this carries over to the G1 stars, or whether the extra false alarms are real (too few events). Nothing in the production detector or the target list was changed. All results, the spec and the code are in experiments/quality_mask/; the Compass review is in research/compass-reviews/2026-10-20-quality-mask.md.

4. Why write the plan down before running the experiment?

So the result can't be bent to fit what we hoped. Rules chosen after seeing the data are too easy to set just below the signal.

5. Raw and cleaned flux show the same transit depth, yet the detector finds the transit only in one. What differs?

The noise estimate. SNR is depth divided by noise; with a larger noise estimate the same depth gives a smaller SNR.

docs.title: 21 October 2026: a progress bar that has to prove itself
docs.text:
Field note · day 3 · about 8 min

In plain words

The home page now has a Mission readiness bar, from 0 to 100. It shows how complete and how well built our plan is. Today it reads 36. It is not the chance of finding a planet, and it can't be raised by feeling: every point needs proof, some points are counted by the program itself, and the book refuses to build if the rules are broken.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. You asked for a progress bar that updates as we learn and get closer to finding a two-sun planet. The first idea, "how close are we to a planet", can't be measured: a careful search that finds nothing is still a finished plan. So the bar measures the plan, and "Candidates found" is a separate counter.
  2. The plan is split into six stages with points that add up to 100: Know the sky (10), Detector (25), Vetting (20), Calibration (10), The search (25), Candidate to paper (10). Each stage is a list of items with a weight, so you can see exactly what is done and what is not (the Progress page).
  3. Three kinds of rule keep it honest:
    • No proof, no points. An item with credit must point to a fact in the claims register or to a file in the repo. If the proof doesn't exist, the book won't build.
    • Some points count themselves. "Stars searched out of 549" fills up by itself when the search writes targets/g1_searched.csv. "SS-0001 exists" turns on when the first real candidate is added.
    • Every change is logged. If I change a credit and forget to write a line saying why, the book won't build. The number can go down if a result is overturned.
  4. The home page status panel is now generated from the same file, so its numbers can't drift away from the truth the way my hand-typed version did.
  5. A small "Book health" line shows pages, labs and facts, and counts stale phrases. An en or em dash anywhere in the book now fails the build, because that is your rule.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text: A good progress measure is checkable. "We're about 40% there" is an opinion. "These 23 items, with these weights, each with proof, add up to 36" is a statement you can argue with, correct, and watch change. The weights are my first draft; they live in one file (book/progress/mission.yml) and you can change any of them.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text: Open book/progress/mission.yml. To raise a credit: change the number, add the proof, and add one line to changes with the date, the points gained and the reason. Then run .venv-docs\Scripts\python.exe book\tools\test_mission.py to check the rules, and build the book.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Today's number is 35.75, shown as 36: Know the sky 10 of 10, Detector 15 of 25, Vetting about 10 of 20, Calibration 1 of 10, the search 0 of 25 (no star of the 549 has been properly searched yet), paper 0 of 10.
  • Tested: the real rules were broken on purpose (no proof, an unlogged change, a stray dash) and each time the book refused to build with a plain message; an untouched copy built fine. The bar was checked on a phone-size screen and a desktop one, in dark and light.
  • Not done: a history graph of the number over time (a later version), and any change to the star hunt, which stays on hold until you say start.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why doesn't a bar that fills toward '100 = planet found' make sense?

Discovery isn't something we control or can measure in advance. A careful search that finds nothing is still a completed plan, so the bar measures the plan and counts candidates separately.

2. What stops someone from just typing a higher number?

Any credit needs proof (a fact or a file that exists), and every change must be logged with a reason that adds up to the total. The book refuses to build otherwise.

docs.title: 23 October 2026: rebuilding the book around a map
docs.text:
Field note · day 5 · about 8 min

In plain words

You told me the book forced labs on you, had no overview and felt disconnected, so we rebuilt it. The home page is now a map of the real sky, with three tabs, optional labs, one review page per Part and a summary at the top of every chapter. Nothing about the science changed, and the star hunt is still on hold.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. You answered 19 rounds of questions, and I wrote them into a design brief (research/BOOK-REDESIGN-BRIEF.md). You approved it and chose font B, Inter.
  2. The home page is a map of the real sky around Cygnus. The six large stars are the six Parts and the small dots around each are its chapters. Behind them are 310 real stars, the Milky Way, a chart grid, and 546 amber specks: our Kepler stars, each at its true place. (Three of our 549 have no position in the catalogue, so the caption says "546 drawn".)
  3. Three tabs, one flat list. The menu is Read, Hunt and Reference. Under Read, the fifteen chapters sit in one list with the Part names as dividers.
  4. Two ways through the same pages. The journey follows the order the project needed each idea; by topic is the textbook order. A button at the end of every chapter switches between them.
  5. Every chapter now opens the same way: a strip showing where you are, a three-line 1-minute summary, then a two-sentence plain-words box. It ends with Mark as read and a Next link that says why you might want it.
  6. Labs are optional. They moved to a "Try it yourself" page at the end of each Part, with the real output first and the commands in a fold. The chapters no longer send you to them.
  7. Questions moved too. The 48 chapter questions now live on one review page per Part ("Check yourself"), where nothing is scored or saved.
  8. Glossary words are tappable. The first time a chapter uses a term, it links to a small popup with the plain definition.
  9. A new look: the Inter font, hosted in the book so it works offline, and text colours made to a 7-to-1 contrast or better. A test now fails if the colours slip below that.
  10. Every chapter opens with a short story, in the personal voice, built only from facts already in the register (Kepler-16, TOI-1338 b and our own days), each with its label. The story of PH1 b waits until its facts are checked.
  11. Two tap-and-drag demos. In Chapter 5, two stars and a planet circle in a top-down view while a light curve is drawn beneath: set the planet's year to the real one (6.52 orbits of the stars) and it says how far apart the crossings land compared with how long each lasts. In Chapter 7, a made-up light curve with a hidden dip lets you turn up the noise, average points together and switch on a slow drift to see why averaging stops helping. In Chapter 2, the real TOI-1338 light curve from sector 98 (10-minute averages) can be dragged and zoomed, from the whole sector down to the 0.2% dip of the planet's crossing.
  12. One small diagram tops every chapter, drawn in the book's own colours (they switch with day and night): one star with three catalogue numbers, a light curve with two kinds of dip, a funnel of dips and tests, and so on.
  13. Credited NASA pictures open Parts 1 to 3 (the Kepler and K2 fields of view, and two artist's concepts of Kepler-16b, each labelled as a drawing and credited). Parts 4 to 6 have no picture yet.
  14. The story of PH1 b, the planet that volunteers found by eye, is on the new Eyes mode page. Its facts come from the paper's abstract (claim F-059, marked LIKELY because only the abstract was read).
  15. A cheat sheet for every Part: one printable page built from the chapters, with three lines per chapter, the words used and the numbers to remember. It prints as plain black on white.
  16. A Listen button on every chapter reads it aloud with your device's own voice (free, works offline, nothing is sent anywhere). It skips pictures, code, tables and the source list, highlights what it is saying, and Pause remembers the place.
  17. Eyes mode, practice version. You see a day and a half of the real TOI-1338 light curve with nothing marked and answer Dip, No dip, Odd or Not sure; then the hidden thing is outlined. Sittings are 5, 20, 50 or 100 light curves. The stretches contain fake dips we hid, glitches, real eclipses and the real planet crossing, so the answer is always known. The real stars of the hunt are not connected: the hunt stays on hold until you say start.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text: A map is a promise about where things are. To draw part of the sky on a flat page you need each star's position (right ascension and declination, like longitude and latitude on the sky) and a rule for flattening a sphere. We used a gnomonic projection, which keeps straight lines straight and distorts only a little over a patch this size. Brightness becomes dot size: a smaller magnitude number means a brighter star, so it gets a bigger dot. Colour comes from the star's spectral type. That is why the map is real: change the catalogue and the picture changes.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text: Open book/data/path.yml: it lists the Parts, the fifteen chapters, their summaries and the journey order. Edit a line, then run .venv-docs\Scripts\python.exe -m mkdocs build --strict inside book, and the map, the strips and the Next links all follow. To redraw the sky from fresh catalogues, book/tools/make_sky.py (needs the internet) rewrites book/data/sky.json.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Tested: the strict build passes; a link checker followed every link and anchor on all 61 built pages; the colour test passes; the home page does not scroll sideways at phone width; the glossary popup, Mark as read and the reading-order switch all worked in the browser.
  • Not done yet: eyes mode on the hunt's real stars (waits for your start), a recorded voice instead of the device voice (a better-sounding tool, your call), and pictures for Parts 4 to 6. They are the next phases in the brief.
  • Not tested: the Listen button was tested with a stand-in voice in a browser with no sound, so how it sounds on your phone is unchecked. You have not read it yet. The real test is your 15 minutes: tell me where you got lost and that goes to the top of the fix list.

docs.title: Later the same night: breaking it on purpose
docs.text:
After the build I tried to break the book, which is where the real lessons were.

  • A tool crashed on our map. The theme rewrites every link on a page when you move between pages, and that code throws an error on links inside an SVG picture, because an SVG link's address is read-only. A screenshot would never show it; a browser test that listens for errors did. The map's links now use the older xlink:href form, and the error is gone.
  • Sizes need a ruler, not an eye. A script measured every tappable thing at phone width. The map's dots were about 15 pixels wide, too small for a thumb, and several links were short. They are now at least 24 pixels (the map) or 44 (everything else), and the check runs before every publish.
  • Numbers must agree on a page. Building the explorer from the real data showed that Chapter 2 gave the primary eclipse as 5.1% and the secondary as 0.4%, while our measured values (claim F-046) are about 6% at the bottom (5.7% typical) and 0.3%. The table now uses the measured values with their label.
  • Facts need their labels even in summaries. The new summaries repeated numbers (14 planets, one in four candidates) without the little VERIFIED chips. They have them now.
  • A rule only counts if you have seen it refuse. Ten deliberately broken copies (a missing chapter, a sidebar that disagrees with the page order, a story that is too long) are each refused by book/tools/test_shape.py. A page nobody links to, a stray dash and a colour that fails 7-to-1 are also caught.

Idea: test the failure, not the happy path. A check you have never seen fail is a hope, not a check.

You could try it: in book/data/path.yml, change one chapter's part and run the build. It stops with a plain message instead of publishing a book whose map and menu disagree.

docs.title: Afternoon: an outside review finds two silent bugs
docs.text:
A separate Claude, with web access and a copy of our code, answered our research brief. Everything went through Compass first: I re-ran each bug here with my own scripts, recounted its numbers from our target files and looked up all 20 of its papers in ADS. All 20 were real (Gemini's answer had 7 of 12 wrong). Full review: research/compass-reviews/2026-10-23-deep-review.md.

  • Bug 1: the detector was blind on 30-minute data. It averages the light into 10-minute bins and ignores any box less than 80% full. With one point every 30 minutes only a third of the bins have data, so every box is ignored. I hid an obvious dip (signal 23 times the noise) in fake data: found at 2, 3.3 and 10-minute spacing, nothing at 30. TESS took 30-minute pictures until 2020, and Kepler's own light curves are 30-minute, so the planned Kepler test would have failed for no real reason.
  • Bug 2: old QLP files used the wrong column. Before sector 56, QLP's flattened column has a different name (kspsap_flux), and the loader picked it. It is the same flattening we had already caught shrinking a 6-hour dip by about 70%. Our one QLP test happened to use sector 98, which has the good column, so it passed.
  • Together they touch about half of the planned QLP data. Nothing has been searched yet, so no result is wrong, but those stars would have looked quiet.
  • The odds moved up a little, to about 20% (range 5 to 45%). The outside estimate was 21 to 39%, but it used the noise of TOI-1338, a quiet star outside our list. Kepler-16, the one star of ours we have measured, is about twice as noisy. With that noise the same sum gives about 17%.
  • Timing matters: TESS looks at the Kepler field again in July and August 2027. A candidate published with a predicted date before then can be checked by TESS itself.

docs.title: Evening: the fixes, and the first look at our own stars' noise
docs.text:
You said to apply the changes and make sure nothing breaks, so the order was: tests first, then fixes, then proof.

  • Tests that fail first. A new check hides a dip at five spacings (2, 3.3, 10, 29.4 and 30 minutes) and reads our real QLP and SPOC files. On the old code it failed at 29.4 minutes; on the new code all of it passes.
  • The fixes. The detector now averages into bins as wide as the data's own spacing when that is slower than 10 minutes. Old QLP sectors use the raw flux (it keeps the dip's depth). A file whose cleaned column is empty now falls back to the raw one instead of returning nothing.
  • Nothing else broke. The old and new detector both ran on all 51 light curves we have: 50 gave exactly the same results, and the one that changed is the old QLP file, as intended.
  • The audit, tried on 7 of our stars. In every sector it hides one standard dip and checks that it comes back: it always did where the noise allowed, and never where it did not. It also measures how much worse than ideal the noise is. The middle value is 1.76 times the ideal, and Kepler-16 is about 1.9, not the 2.8 I quoted this afternoon: that number came from a different way of measuring. So the odds lean a little up, but these 7 stars are brighter than most of ours, so I keep about 20% until all 549 are measured.
  • One honest letdown: the old QLP sectors keep their dips now, but their raw flux is about six times noisier than SPOC's. Those sectors will count for little until we find a better way to clean them.

docs.title: Night: the Kepler test
docs.text:
With the 30-minute bug fixed, the detector could finally read the original Kepler data. We downloaded four years of it for Kepler-16, 34 and 35 (52 files, 21 MB). No list of the exact transit times could be opened, so I found the transits a different way first, and checked each one by eye: 7 for Kepler-16, 7 for Kepler-34 and 4 for Kepler-35. Then the real detector ran blind. It found all 18, in both kinds of flux, at 13 to 320 times the noise. Most of its extra events sat at the edges of Kepler's monthly pauses, which our rules already flag for a person. One extra dip happened at the same moment on two different stars, which can only be the spacecraft. The honest limit: the transits I could see by eye are the easy ones, so this is not yet a fair race against Davies et al., who counted 9 for Kepler-34 and 7 for Kepler-35.

Idea: a filter that silently returns nothing looks exactly like a quiet star. Every way the data can come in (each product, spacing and era) needs a test that hides a known dip and fails loudly if it does not come back.

You could try it: research/deep-review-2026-10-23/our-checks/verify_b1_b2.py prints the four spacings and which column the loader picks for each QLP file we have.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do bigger dots mean brighter stars on the map?

Magnitude is backwards: a smaller number is brighter. The map turns that into a dot size, so the brightest stars (like Deneb) are drawn largest.

2. Why does the caption say 546 drawn, not 549?

Three of our stars have no sky position in the Villanova Kepler catalogue, and we only draw what we can place. The book says so rather than rounding up.

3. Why did a dip that was obvious at 10-minute spacing vanish at 30-minute spacing?

The detector only trusted boxes that were at least 80% full of 10-minute bins. At 30-minute spacing two bins in three are empty, so no box ever qualified and the search returned nothing, with no error.

docs.title: Lab 0: your workbench
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 10 min · Level L0

In plain words

Before you can look at stars yourself, your PC needs the right tools: Python (a programming language) and a few astronomy toolkits. They're already installed in the project folder on D:. In this lab you open a terminal, run one check, and read what it tells you.

Goal: run your first command and confirm the workbench is ready.

docs.title: What you need to know first
docs.text:
• A terminal is a window where you type commands instead of clicking. On Windows it's called PowerShell.
  • Python runs our scripts. The project has its own copy, with all the toolkits, at D:\second-sun\.venv. A copy like this is called a virtual environment: it keeps the project's tools separate from everything else on your PC.
  • Why D:? Your C: drive is nearly full. Every lab keeps downloads and temporary files on D:. The file labs/_env.py, which every lab loads first, makes sure of that.

The toolkits you'll meet:

Toolkit What it does numpy fast maths on long lists of numbers (a light curve is a long list) astropy astronomy basics: times, coordinates, the FITS file format lightkurve finds, downloads and plots TESS and Kepler light curves astroquery asks NASA's archives questions (like "which star is this?") matplotlib draws graphs wotan flattens slow wiggles out of a light curve (Chapter 8) batman draws a perfect planet transit, used to make fake planets (Chapter 9)

docs.text:

You type a star's name. docs.text:
The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab1_name_to_number.py "Kepler-16"

It takes about 20 seconds, because it's asking NASA's servers over the internet.

docs.title: Reading it line by line
docs.text:
• Three names, one star. TIC is TESS's catalogue number, KIC is Kepler's, and the Gaia number is from the European star map (Chapter 1). Our G1 list stores the KIC and the TIC for every star.
  • Position. RA and Dec are the sky's longitude and latitude. Dec +51.8° puts Kepler-16 in the northern sky, in the constellation Cygnus, inside Kepler's old field.
  • TESS magnitude 10.94. About 100 times too faint to see with your eyes (Chapter 1), but bright for TESS. Our G1 list goes down to 13.5.
  • 4018 K, 0.77 Suns. The catalogue treats the light as one star. Kepler-16 is really two stars too close together to separate, so these are blended values.
  • Neighbours. A TESS pixel is 21 arcseconds wide LIKELY, so a star within 1 arcminute shares pixels with ours. Four neighbours bright enough to matter means a dip could come from one of them. That's why Chapter 11 exists.
  • 94 light curves. Six different teams turned the same TESS pictures into light curves. SPOC is NASA's own and the best. QLP is MIT's, made for many more stars (Chapter 3). SPOC has 26 files for 17 sectors because some sectors have both a 2-minute and a 20-second version.
  • Sectors 14 to 83, with gaps. TESS came back to this part of the sky in 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and from late 2023 through 2024 (years checked in the archive's search table).

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
Open labs\lab1_name_to_number.py in Notepad and follow along:

  1. Catalogs.query_object(name, radius=2/60, catalog="TIC") asks for every TIC star within 2 arcminutes of the name's position.
  2. It sorts them by distance and takes the closest: our star. The others are the neighbours.
  3. lk.search_lightcurve(f"TIC {star['ID']}") asks MAST which light curves exist, and the loop groups them by team.

docs.title: Do it yourself
docs.text:
The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab2_get_the_data.py "Kepler-16" 82

The 82 is the sector. Downloads go to D:\second-sun\data\labs (never C:). If the file is already there, it isn't downloaded again.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
The file name packs in the facts: tess2024223182411 is when the data was processed (year 2024, day 223), s0082 is the sector, 0000000299096355 is the TIC number, and _lc means light curve.

The file format is FITS, astronomy's standard since 1981. A FITS file has a header (labels: which star, which camera) and tables (the data).

The header says this star fell on camera 3, chip (CCD) 4. Stars on the same chip share spacecraft problems, which is how the QLP fix borrows good time windows from neighbours (Chapter 3).

The columns you'll use most:

Column Meaning TIME when, in BTJD: days since a fixed moment in 2014 (BJD 2457000). BTJD 3533 is August 2024 SAP_FLUX raw brightness: all the light in the star's pixels, in electrons per second PDCSAP_FLUX cleaned brightness: NASA removed known spacecraft effects. We use this first ..._ERR the expected noise on each measurement QUALITY a warning number; 0 means fine (see below) MOM_CENTR1/2 where the star's light centre sits on the chip; it moves if the telescope wobbles SAP_BKG the background sky light that was subtracted

18,619 cadences. A cadence is one measurement. 25.9 days × 720 per day (one every 2 minutes) is about 18,650, so almost none are missing.

PDCSAP is missing on 482 rows: exactly the 482 flagged ones (checked row by row). NASA blanks the cleaned flux where it doesn't trust the data.

The QUALITY number is a set of switches added together. Each switch is a power of 2:

Value Name (from lightkurve) Meaning 8 Earth point the spacecraft turned toward Earth to send data home 16 Argabrightening a sudden glow across the whole camera (cause uncertain) 32 Desaturation event momentum dump: thrusters fired LIKELY 128 Manual exclude NASA's team marked these by hand 2048, 4096 Straylight scattered light from Earth or Moon (not in this file; common in others)

This file contains the values 8, 16, 32, 40, 128 and 160 (checked by script). A value of 40 means 32 + 8: a thruster firing and an Earth-point moment; 160 is 128 + 32. The 16 momentum-dump cadences matter: on 20 October our first G1 dip turned out to be the telescope wobbling just before one (Chapter 10).

docs.title: Lab 3: plot a light curve and measure its noise
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 20 min · Level L1 · after Lab 2 and Chapter 2

In plain words

You draw the Kepler-16 file from Lab 2 as a graph, raw and cleaned, with the thruster firings marked. Then the script measures how much the brightness wobbles when you average 10 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours or 6 hours of data. That table is how you judge whether a dip is real (Chapter 7).

Goal: see a real light curve with your own eyes, and measure its noise the way our search does.

The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab3_plot_and_read.py

Then open the picture it saves: D:\second-sun\labs\out\lab3_tic299096355.png.

docs.title: Reading the picture
docs.text:
• The deep drop near BTJD 3552 is the two stars eclipsing each other: the small star passes in front of the big one. It's about 8 to 12% deep, far deeper than any planet. The binary's period is 41.08 days, so a 26-day sector catches at most one of each kind.
  • Raw vs cleaned. The raw curve drifts and jumps at each gap. NASA's cleaning flattens those drifts, but look just after the eclipse: the cleaned curve spikes up where the raw one doesn't. Cleaning can create problems as well as remove them.
  • The small bump near 3544 in the raw data is gone in the cleaned data. Something on the camera, not the star.
  • The red lines are thruster firings, about every 6 days LIKELY. One sits right at the end of the eclipse, exactly where the cleaned curve spikes: two problems in one place, so that stretch needs care.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
• 2 min: one measurement wobbles by about 2,000 ppm (0.2%).
  • "If white" is what averaging should give if every wobble were independent: divide by √N (Chapter 7).
  • Measured stays much higher. Over 1 hour it's 908 ppm, not 368. Slow wobbles don't average away. That's red noise, and it's why a 5-hour planet dip of 1,000 ppm would be hard to see here.

Why this lab corrected our own number

While building this lab I found that an earlier estimate of Kepler-16's one-hour noise (236 ppm) used a quick method that flattens away most of the slow wobble. The real figure for our search is about 900 ppm VERIFIED. Chapter 7 tells the story; it's logged in the mistakes register.

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. Reads the file and finds the binary's period in our G1 list by the TIC number.
  2. Plots raw and cleaned brightness, divided by their middle value so 1.0 means "normal".
  3. Keeps only quality-0 rows, flattens slow trends with the same 2-day filter our detector uses, and masks the eclipses.
  4. For each bin size, averages groups of points and measures the spread with a robust method (it ignores a few wild points).

docs.text: You see Why Fix IndexError at the start No Kepler-16 sector 82 file yet Do Lab 2 first binary period from G1 list: None The star isn't in G1 Fine; eclipses just won't be masked

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• The warning line: 37% of this sector is thrown away by the quality filter. That's a lot, and it's mostly scattered light (Lab 2's bits 2048 and 4096). Compass flagged this: some of that data could be kept with a warning instead. It's on the list.
  • 15.1% masked: TOI-1338's stars eclipse every 14.6 days, and each eclipse plus a safety margin is cut out. A planet crossing during an eclipse is lost (Chapter 9 measured about 1 in 11).
  • One event, SNR 8.5, 5 hours, 1,989 ppm, at BTJD 4025.638 VERIFIED. That's 16 December 2025, the crossing a 2024 paper predicted VERIFIED. A 1,989 ppm dip on a star 1.25 times the Sun's size means a planet about 6 Earth radii across (Chapter 2's depth formula), close to TOI-1338 b's published size VERIFIED.
  • Could you see it by eye? In the middle panel, honestly, barely. In the zoom, yes: about 0.2% lower for a few hours. That's why we need a search with a measured false-alarm rate (Chapter 7) rather than eyes alone.

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. load() reads the file, uses the cleaned flux and drops flagged rows.
  2. eclipse_mask_auto() folds the data at the binary's 14.6-day period, finds both eclipses, and masks them.
  3. find_events(..., thr=THR) is the detector from Chapter 8: flatten with a 2-day filter, average into 10-minute bins, slide boxes of 3 to 15 hours, and keep anything more than 7 times the measured noise.
