docs.title: Lab 5: two suns up close
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 15 min · Level L4 · after Chapter 6

In plain words

You take one month of TOI-1338 data and "fold" it: cut it into 14.6-day pieces (one orbit of the two stars) and stack them. Both eclipses line up and become easy to see and measure. This is how our search finds and hides the stars' own eclipses before looking for a planet.

Goal: see both eclipses of a real binary, measure them, and see what gets masked.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Folded 25321 measurements at P = 14.6086 d. Eclipses found: 2
  phase 0.509: depth 5.67%, width about 5.3 h
  phase 0.963: depth 0.32%, width about 5.3 h
Second eclipse comes 0.453 of an orbit after the first (0.500 would mean a circular orbit)
Masked before searching: 15.1% of the data
Picture saved: D:\second-sun\labs\out\lab5_toi1338_fold.png
TOI-1338, sector 98, folded at 14.6086 days, from your PC VERIFIED. Red: masked. Middle: the primary eclipse. Right: the secondary.

docs.title: Do it yourself
docs.text:
The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab5_two_suns.py

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Phase is where in the stars' orbit a measurement sits, from 0 to 1. Folding puts all orbits on top of each other.
  • The deep eclipse (phase 0.509): the small star passes in front of the big one and blocks about 6% of the light at the bottom. The script reports 5.67%, the typical value inside the masked stretch. With Chapter 2's formula, √0.06 ≈ 0.24: the small star is about a quarter of the big one's size.
  • The shallow eclipse (phase 0.963): the big star hides the small, faint one. Only 0.3% of the light disappears, because the small star gives so little light.
  • 0.453, not 0.5: the orbit is stretched (Chapter 6).
  • The gap from phase 0.02 to 0.35. Look at the picture: almost no data there. The quality filter dropped 37% of this sector (Lab 4), mostly scattered light that returns once per TESS orbit. TESS's own orbit (13.7 days) is close to the stars' 14.6 days, so the dropped stretches likely keep landing on the same part of the stars' orbit. A planet crossing during that part of the orbit would be invisible in this sector.
  • 15.1% masked: each eclipse plus a safety margin of 1.5 times its width on both sides. Any planet crossing in there is lost to the search (Chapter 9: about 1 in 11).

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. eclipse_mask_auto() (in pipeline/detect_v2.py) folds at the period, takes the middle value in 600 phase slices, and flags slices more than 4 times the noise below normal. Each flagged run is an eclipse.
  2. The script measures each eclipse's typical depth, its phase and its width, then draws the fold and two zooms.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab6_fake_planets.py

It runs the full search 20 times, so give it a few minutes.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• R+ means Earth radii. depth is the textbook depth, (planet size ÷ star size)².
  • 6 and 8 Earth radii: found every time. 5: once in 4. 3 and 4: never. Same floor as the bigger tests in Chapter 9.
  • Depth kept compares the dip's centre after cleaning with the fake's real centre depth. 92 to 96% for the big ones: cleaning barely touches them.
  • Why 129% and 109% for the small ones? Their dips are smaller than the noise, so "depth kept" is mostly noise. A number can be computed and still mean nothing: check the size of the signal against the noise before reading a ratio.
  • The picture: the 5-Earth-radius dip at 4013.0 is real, but you'd hardly pick it out by eye. The search found it there and not at the other three times: at the edge of the floor, luck (where the noise happens to wobble) decides.

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. Loads sector 98 and masks the stars' eclipses (as in Lab 4).
  2. For each size and time, transit() uses batman to draw a realistic transit (a 95.2-day orbit, a star 1.25 times the Sun, limb darkening), and multiplies the real light curve by it, because a planet blocks a fraction of the light.
  3. Runs find_events() and counts the fake as found if an event sits within 6 hours of where it was hidden.
  4. Cleans the data and compares the dip's centre with the fake's true centre depth.

docs.title: Lab 7: is the dip on that star?
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 20 min · Level L6 · after Chapter 11

In plain words

You open TOI-1338's pixel file (a small movie: 11 × 11 pixels, one frame every 2 minutes) and compare the frames during the planet's crossing with the frames around it. Which pixels got dimmer? Did the centre of the light move? Which catalogued stars sit on these pixels? This is the check that catches a neighbour pretending to be a planet.

Goal: check for yourself that a dip is on the right star.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Pixel file: 11 x 11 pixels, 25321 pictures, aperture of 7 pixels
Dimming summed over the aperture: 3029 ppm
Brightest pixel (the star): row 4, col 4. Most-dimmed pixel: row 4, col 5
Centroid shift during the crossing: +0.001" in row (+0.1 x the chance spread), -0.000" in column (-0.0 x)
Chance spread measured from 128 fake windows: 0.006" (row), 0.012" (column)
Catalogued stars brighter than Tmag 16 on these pixels: 8
  TIC 260128333: Tmag 11.5, 0" from our star
  TIC 260128339: Tmag 12.8, 103" from our star
  TIC 260128334: Tmag 14.0, 60" from our star

  TIC 737409352: Tmag 14.2, 59" from our star

From your PC VERIFIED.

docs.text:
The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab7_pixels.py

It reads a 50 MB file already on D: and asks MAST for the neighbours, so give it a minute.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Aperture of 7 pixels: SPOC adds up these 7 pixels (white outline) to make the light curve.
  • Dimming 3,029 ppm summed over the aperture: more than the cleaned light curve's 1,989 ppm (Lab 4). These are raw pixels with no cleaning, and this crossing comes just after a data gap, where the light is probably still settling (scattered light). Raw numbers need care.
  • Brightest pixel and most-dimmed pixel are neighbours (columns 4 and 5): the dimming is on our star.
  • Centroid shift: about zero, compared with a chance spread measured from 128 quiet windows. Chapter 11 works out that a neighbour 60″ away would have moved it about 0.12″: 10 to 20 times the chance spread.
  • The neighbours: the 12.8-magnitude star 103″ away is the bright patch at upper left in the picture, and it doesn't dim. The three 14th-magnitude stars about 60″ away sit right of the aperture.
  • Your own star is listed first, at 0″, with Tmag 11.5.

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. lk.read() opens the pixel file, dropping flagged frames.
  2. Frames within 0.12 days of the crossing are "in"; frames 0.22 to 0.72 days away are "out". out − in per pixel is the difference image.
  3. estimate_centroids() gives the light's centre in every frame. The shift is the median in minus the median out, times 21″ per pixel.
  4. The chance spread: the same measurement repeated every quarter day across the sector (away from the crossing), and the robust spread of all those fake shifts.
  5. Neighbours come from the TIC; tpf.wcs (the file's map from sky to pixels) places them on the picture.

docs.title: Lab 8: read STANLEY's output
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 15 min · Level L5 · after Chapter 12

In plain words

STANLEY already searched TOI-1338 on your PC (33 minutes, on 20 October). Its result is a big table: one score for each of 20,482 guessed planet orbits. This lab reads that table, prints the best orbits, and draws a picture, so you can judge the result yourself.

Goal: read a professional search result and decide how much to trust it.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Grid: 173 trial periods from 90.05 to 100.03 days x up to 123 starting angles = 20482 orbits tried
  period  96.11 d: best score  18.4 sigma
  period  96.16 d: best score  16.3 sigma
  period  93.84 d: best score  12.1 sigma
  period  99.41 d: best score  11.4 sigma
  period  96.28 d: best score  10.8 sigma
Typical score (median): 4.2 sigma; scores above 5 sigma: 28% of all orbits
TOI-1338 b's published period: 95.2 days (Kostov et al. 2020)
Picture saved: D:\second-sun\labs\out\lab8_stanley_toi1338.png
STANLEY on TOI-1338, from your PC VERIFIED.

docs.title: Do it yourself
docs.text:
The commands, when you are at your PC 
cd D:\second-sun
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe labs\lab8_read_stanley.py

It only reads files, so it takes a few seconds. (Re-running the search itself takes about 33 minutes; that's optional, later.)

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Three of the top five sit within about 1 day of the real planet (96.11, 96.16, 96.28). That clustering is a good sign: a real signal is strong over a small patch of guesses, not at one lucky point.
  • 93.84 and 99.41 days score 11 to 12σ. Are those planets? Almost certainly not: they're how high noise and leftover wiggles can reach in 20,482 tries.
  • The histogram's tall bar at 0: about 3,400 orbits have a score of exactly 0. STANLEY's output doesn't say why (an orbit it skipped, or one with no crossings during the data are the likely reasons, but not confirmed). They're counted in the 28%, so the true share of noise orbits above 5σ is a little higher.
  • The hump at 4 to 5σ: that's what "nothing" looks like in this search. A score has to stand well clear of it.

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. The trial periods. STANLEY saves its grid as a text file. The script pulls out every number and keeps those between 85 and 105 days (stored in seconds).
  2. The scores. A numpy file with one row per period and one column per starting angle. -29 marks unused cells (some periods have fewer angles), which become "missing".
  3. It reports each period's best score, the typical score, and draws both panels.

Why step 1 matters

STANLEY's log prints the period range from high to low, and our first reading assumed the table ran that way: wrong, giving 93.8 days. The saved grid runs low to high, and the number of angles per period (114 rising to 123) matches the table row by row. That's how we know the order. Lesson: read the axis from the data file, not from a log message.

docs.title: Lab 9: your own star
docs.text:
Lab · at your PC · about 30 min · Level L6 · the final lab

In plain words

This is the whole route on a real G1 star, start to finish: look it up, download its data, find and hide the two stars' eclipses, search for dips, check the dips against upside-down data and spacecraft events, and list what's left for a human to judge. SPOC 2-minute sectors available: 9; using the first 3

docs.text:
• 2 eclipses found, 19.4% masked. Both of the binary's eclipses were found from Kepler's period alone, by folding all three sectors together. One sector is often too short to pin down a long-period binary, which is why the lab folds them all at once (the lesson from Kepler-16, Chapter 10).
  • 0 events, 0 in the flipped data. A bright (9.8 mag), quiet star. Nothing crossed the bar.
  • What "nothing" means here: no single crossing bigger than roughly 5 to 6 Earth radii (Chapter 9's floor, for a star this bright or brighter) in the unmasked 80% of three sectors. It does not mean no planet: a small one, or one that crossed during the masked 19.4% or between sectors, would be missed.

docs.title: How the script works
docs.text:
1. Finds your star in the G1 list (its period and Kepler number).
  2. Searches MAST for SPOC 2-minute light curves and downloads the first few (Lab 2), logging each.
  3. Folds all sectors at the binary's period to find and mask both eclipses (Lab 5).
  4. For each sector: runs the search (Lab 4), runs it again on upside-down data (Chapter 8), reads the gaps and thruster firings, and applies the rules: events also found upside down are rejected; events near gaps or firings get flags (Chapter 10).
  5. Prints what's left and saves a picture of each event.

docs.title: When an event does appear
docs.text:
Ask, in this order (the short version of Chapter 10):

  1. Flags? Near a gap edge or a thruster firing: suspect, look at the raw data around it.
  2. Shape: a dip with a flat or curved bottom, not a single spike or a step.
  3. Near an eclipse? A dip just outside the red masked region may be the eclipse's edge.
  4. Second product (rule C8): is it in QLP or TESS-SPOC data too?
  5. Pixels (Chapter 11): is it on our star?

docs.title: Learning track
docs.text:
Seven levels · one or two sittings each · your progress line updates when you finish one

In plain words

Seven levels take you from "what is a light curve?" to being the second key: someone who can check a candidate independently. Each level says what to read, which lab to do on your PC, and ends with three questions. When you can answer them, tell me "L2 done, 3/3" (or whatever level), and I'll set the date on your progress line.

Level 0 of 6 · Next: L0 What a light curve is

docs.title: L0 · What a light curve is
docs.text:
Read: Chapter 1, then Chapter 2 sections 2.1 to 2.2. Do: Lab 0, Lab 1, Lab 2.

L0 check 1. What do the columns TIME, PDCSAP_FLUX and QUALITY hold?

When each measurement was taken (BTJD days), the cleaned brightness, and a warning number (0 = fine).

L0 check 2. Kepler-16 is TIC 299096355 and KIC 12644769. Why two numbers?

TESS and Kepler each made their own catalogue. The TIC finds the TESS data; the KIC links to Kepler's binary catalogue.

L0 check 3. Magnitude 10 vs magnitude 15: which is brighter, and how much?

Magnitude 10, by 5 magnitudes: 100 times.

docs.title: L1 · How big is the dip?
docs.text:
Read: the L1 lesson (or Chapter 2, section 2.3). Do: Lab 3.

L1 check 1. A dip goes from 1.000 to 0.998. How deep is it in ppm and in percent?

0.002 = 2,000 ppm = 0.2%.

L1 check 2. In Lab 3, Kepler-16's eclipse was about 10% deep. Could that be a planet?

No. √0.10 ≈ 0.32: something a third of the star's size. That's a star (the companion), not a planet.

L1 check 3. Why do we divide the flux by its median before measuring a dip?

So 1.0 means "normal" and a dip reads directly as a fraction, whatever the star's raw brightness.

docs.title: L2 · From dip depth back to size
docs.text:
Read: Chapter 2 sections 2.3 and 2.5; Chapter 11 section 11.3 (dilution). Do: the "Reading it" part of Lab 4.

L2 check 1. A 1,000 ppm dip on a star the size of the Sun. How big is the planet?

√0.001 ≈ 0.032 of the Sun's radius; the Sun is 109 Earths across, so about 3.4 Earth radii.

L2 check 2. The same dip, but only 80% of the light is from our star. True depth?

1,000 ÷ 0.8 = 1,250 ppm, so the planet is √(1/0.8) ≈ 1.12 times bigger than the first estimate.

L2 check 3. Why is a transit's centre deeper than (planet ÷ star)²?

Limb darkening: the star's middle is brighter than its edge, so blocking the middle removes more light.

docs.title: L3 · Bright stars, faint stars, noise
docs.text:
Read: Chapter 7, Chapter 8. Do: Lab 3's noise table, Lab 4.

L3 check 1. White noise of 2,000 ppm per 2 minutes. Expected wobble of a 2-hour average?

2,000 ÷ √60 ≈ 260 ppm.

L3 check 2. Lab 3 measured 908 ppm for 1 hour where white noise predicts 368. Name the effect.

Red noise: slow drifts that don't average away.

L3 check 3. In Lab 4 at SNR 5, a second event appeared, 15 hours long, next to a data gap. Trust it?

No: it's below our bar, it's at a gap edge, and lowering the bar is exactly how noise gets in (Chapter 7's look-elsewhere effect).

docs.title: L4 · Orbits, and why our dips wander
docs.text:
Read: Chapter 4, Chapter 5, Chapter 6. Do: Lab 5.

L4 check 1. Why do a two-star planet's crossings change length?

The star moves too. Moving with the planet: slow pass, long crossing. Against it: quick pass, short crossing.

L4 check 2. A binary's critical period is 60 days. Search for 40-day planets?

No: closer than the critical orbit, a planet can't survive.

L4 check 3. Why aren't TOI-1338's eclipses exactly half an orbit apart?

The stars' orbit is eccentric (stretched).

docs.title: L5 · The fakes
docs.text:
Read: Chapter 9, Chapter 10 sections 10.1 to 10.2. Do: Lab 6, Lab 8.

L5 check 1. Name three things that can fake a planet's dip.

Any three of: a thruster firing or pointing jitter, a data-gap edge, scattered light, an eclipsing neighbour (blend), the binary's own eclipse edge, stellar variability, noise.

L5 check 2. Why does our search also run on upside-down data?

To count how often noise alone crosses the bar with the same number of tries.

L5 check 3. 28% of STANLEY's orbits scored above 5σ. What does that mean for its 18.4σ peak?

Its σ scale isn't calibrated: noise scores high here. The peak is encouraging but needs calibrating before it means anything precise.

docs.title: L6 · Two-key vetting
docs.text:
Read: Chapter 10 sections 10.3 to 10.6, Chapter 11, Chapter 12. Do: Lab 7, Lab 9.

L6 check 1. A dip appears in SPOC data but not in QLP data at the same time. What does rule C8 say?

It fails C8: a real dip should show in a second, independently made product.

L6 check 2. The light's centre shifted 0.10″; the chance spread is 0.01″. On-target expectation 0.001″. Verdict?

Suspicious: the shift is 10 times the chance spread and far above the on-target expectation, so a neighbour may be the source.

L6 check 3. What does 'second key' mean?

You independently check a candidate and decide whether you agree, before anything is submitted. Both keys must turn.

docs.title: L1 How big is the dip?
docs.text:
Level 1 of 6 · 20 min · Maths: fractions, percentages, ppm, squares

In plain words

When a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a small circle of light. How much light it blocks tells you how big the planet is compared with the star. By the end of this level, Ahmed, you'll be able to look at a dip and say "that's planet-sized" or "that's a whole star".

docs.title: Why this matters for you
docs.text: Most dips in your G1 binaries are the two stars eclipsing each other. The first thing you'll do with any new dip, for the rest of the project, is ask: is it deep enough to be a star? This level gives you that test.

docs.title: The one idea
docs.text:
The fraction of light blocked is the depth:

depth = (planet radius ÷ star radius)²

Radius means centre to edge. It's squared because what's blocked is an area, and area grows with the square of the size. Double the planet's size and the dip gets four times deeper.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
1. A planet half as wide as its star. What depth?

(1/2)² = 1/4 = 25%. That's far too big for a planet; it's the size of a star. When a dip is that deep, think "eclipsing binary", not "planet".

2. You double the planet's size. What happens to the depth?

It goes up 4× (2² = 4).

3. Why do small red stars help us find small planets?

The star is smaller, so the same planet blocks a bigger fraction: the dip is deeper and easier to see.

Summary: depth = (planet ÷ star)². Tiny dips (ppm) can be planets; huge dips (tens of %) are stars.

docs.title: Words to know
docs.text:
• Kepler: NASA's space telescope that stared at one patch of sky from 2009 to 2013 and found thousands of planets and eclipsing binaries.
  • TESS: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018.
  • KIC: Kepler Input Catalog number: Kepler's ID for a star, like KIC 12644769 for Kepler-16.
  • TIC: TESS Input Catalog number: TESS's ID for a star, like TIC 299096355 for Kepler-16.
  • Gaia: The European Space Agency's star-mapping spacecraft.
  • Transit: A planet passing in front of its star as seen from Earth, which makes a small dip in the light curve.
  • Arcsecond: A tiny angle: 1/3,600 of a degree.

  • BTJD: The TESS clock, in days: Barycentric Julian Date minus 2,457,000.
  • TOI: TESS Object of Interest: a signal NASA's team thinks might be a planet.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Stars, names and missions

Read the chapter

1. Star A is magnitude 8, star B is magnitude 13. Which is brighter, and by how much?

A, by 5 magnitudes: 100 times brighter.

2. Why does our G1 list need both the KIC and the TIC number?

The binary's period and eclipse times come from Kepler's catalogue (KIC); the TESS data is filed under the TIC number. We need both to connect the two.

3. A TESS pixel is 21″. A neighbour sits 30″ from our star. Could its light get into our star's pixels?

Yes. 30″ is less than 2 pixels, and a star's light spreads over a few pixels. That's why Chapter 11 checks where a dip really comes from.

4. What's the BTJD of BJD 2,460,295?

2,460,295 − 2,457,000 = 3,295.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Light curves
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. A dip is 1% deep. Roughly how big is the planet compared with its star?

√0.01 = 0.1, so about a tenth of the star's radius. Around a Sun-sized star, that's about Jupiter's size.

2. What's the difference between SAP and PDCSAP?

SAP is the raw summed light; PDCSAP has known spacecraft effects removed. We trust PDCSAP first and use SAP to fill its gaps.

3. TOI-1338's 5% dips repeat every 14.6 days. Planet or star?

Star. 5% means an object about √0.05 ≈ 0.22 of the big star's radius: the small companion star, eclipsing on the binary's 14.6-day orbit.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Our data
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. Why do we need a dip in two different light-curve products?

Each pipeline cleans data differently. A dip in only one could be created by that pipeline's cleaning, not by the star.

2. A light curve is 2 MB. Roughly how much space do 550 stars × 10 sectors take?

550 × 10 × 2 MB = 11,000 MB ≈ 11 GB. Easy for D:.

3. Why are TESS's big pixels a problem for planet hunters?

A faint eclipsing binary next to our star can sit in the same pixel and leak its dips into our light curve, faking a small planet.

docs.title: Words to know
docs.text:
• Circumbinary planet: A planet that orbits both stars of a pair.
  • Binary star: Two stars held together by gravity, each circling their shared centre.
  • Kepler: NASA's space telescope that stared at one patch of sky from 2009 to 2013 and found thousands of planets and eclipsing binaries.
  • TESS: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018.
  • Transit: A planet passing in front of its star as seen from Earth, which makes a small dip in the light curve.

  • SPOC: NASA's Science Processing Operations Center: makes the cleanest TESS light curves, from 2-minute postage stamps.
  • Sector: One TESS stretch of about 27 days looking at the same patch of sky.
  • N-body simulation: A computer calculation that moves several objects (like two stars and a planet) step by step under each other's gravity.
  • STANLEY: A search tool by David Martin's group (Martin et al.

• 14 transiting circumbinary planets are known: 12 from Kepler and 2 from TESS (TOI-1338 b and TIC 172900988 b) VERIFIED

  • The innermost transiting circumbinary planets sit at only 1.3 to 1.6 times the critical period (TOI-1338 b: 1.34) VERIFIED

docs.title: Chapter 4: Two suns
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. What's the difference between an S-type and a P-type planet?

S-type orbits one star of the pair. P-type (circumbinary) orbits both. We hunt P-type.

2. A binary has a period of 10 days. Roughly where would you expect its innermost stable planet?

The critical period is 4 to 7 times the binary period: 40 to 70 days. Known planets pile up at 1.3 to 1.6 times that, so roughly 50 to 110 days.

3. A planet sits at 4 times the stars' separation. About how many binary periods does it take to orbit once?

43/2 = √(4³) = √64 = 8 binary periods.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Wandering transits
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. Why can't we fold a two-sun planet's light curve at one period?

Its transit times shift by up to days, so the dips don't line up at any single period.

2. TOI-1338 b's transits lasted 0.3, 0.4 and 0.6 days. What causes the difference?

The crossed star's own motion. Moving with the planet makes a long transit; moving against it makes a short one.

3. In one sentence, what is G1?

Searching Kepler's eclipsing binaries in newer TESS data for planets that weren't crossing during Kepler but have switched on since, because their orbits precessed.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Orbits and the three-body problem
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. A planet orbits a pair of 1-Sun-total stars at 1 AU. How long is its year?

P² = 1³ / 1 = 1, so 1 year. Same as Earth around the Sun: Kepler's law only cares about the total mass inside.

2. Why are TOI-1338's two eclipses 0.453 of an orbit apart, not 0.5?

The stars' orbit is eccentric (stretched). The stars move faster when close together, so the time from one eclipse to the next is shorter one way round.

3. A binary has a critical period of 50 days. Should we search for planets with 30-day orbits?

No. Planets that close would be unstable and wouldn't survive. Start at 50 days.

4. Why might one crossing last 6 hours and the next 12?

The star moves too. When it moves the same way as the planet, they pass each other slowly (long crossing); in opposite directions, quickly (short crossing).

docs.title: Words to know
docs.text:
• Red noise: Slow wobbles where neighbouring measurements move together.
  • Photon noise: The natural wobble in counting particles of light: like raindrops in a bucket, a count of N varies by about √N.
  • Scattered light: Sunlight bounced off Earth or the Moon into TESS's cameras, raising the background.
  • Quality flag: A number stored with each measurement that warns about problems (thruster firing, scattered light...).
  • White noise: Random wobble where each measurement is independent.
  • TESS: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018.
  • Transit: A planet passing in front of its star as seen from Earth, which makes a small dip in the light curve.
  • SNR: Signal-to-noise ratio: how big a signal is compared with normal wobble.
  • Depth: How much of the star's light a dip blocks, as a fraction: depth = (planet radius ÷ star radius)².
  • Sector: One TESS stretch of about 27 days looking at the same patch of sky.
  • ppm: Parts per million.
  • Robust spread: A measure of wobble that ignores a few wild points: 1.4826 times the median distance from the median.

• Correlated (red) noise makes transit detection much harder than white-noise estimates suggest; detection thresholds must use the noise measured on the transit's own timescale LIKELY
  • NASA's SPOC pipeline only flags a planet after at least two transits and a detection statistic (MES) above 7.1 LIKELY
  • Run on upside-down (flipped) TOI-1338 light curves, detector v2 at SNR 7 still finds 6 fake dips in 10 sectors, with peaks up to SNR 12.6 VERIFIED
  • On TOI-1338 sector 98, detector v2 finds injected 6.4-hour transits of 6 Earth radii 5 times in 7 and of 7 Earth radii every time; 5 Earth radii and smaller are missed VERIFIED

docs.title: Chapter 7: Noise and statistics
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. One point wobbles by 1,000 ppm. With white noise, what does a 4-hour average (120 points) wobble by?

1,000 / √120 ≈ 91 ppm.

2. You measure 400 ppm for that 4-hour average instead. What does that tell you?

The noise is red: slow drifts that don't average away. A dip must be judged against 400 ppm, not 91.

3. Why does running the search on upside-down data help?

It makes the same number of tries on data with no real dips. Whatever it finds shows how often noise alone crosses the bar: the look-elsewhere effect, measured.

4. Why not just flatten with a 3-hour window to get rid of red noise?

It would also flatten the planet: a 6-to-15-hour two-star transit would be partly removed.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Our detector
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. Why did v1's 1-day flattening window hurt us?

A 6-hour dip is a quarter of a day. A 1-day moving fit partly follows the dip down and "flattens" it away, making it shallower than it really is.

2. Why do we search flipped (upside-down) data?

Real dips become bumps, so anything found there is noise or spacecraft effects. It measures our false-alarm rate instead of guessing it.

3. The search finds nothing in a star. What can you say?

Only that no transit stronger than our bar happened in that data: roughly nothing bigger than ~6 Earth radii for a TOI-1338-like star. Smaller planets, or planets not crossing during that sector, could still be there.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Fake planets
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. Why must fakes go in before cleaning, not after?

Cleaning can flatten part of a real dip. Injecting after cleaning would skip that damage, so the test would look better than reality.

2. 3 of 4 fakes found. What's the uncertainty?

√(0.75 × 0.25 / 4) ≈ 0.22: 75% ± 22%. Four trials are far too few.

3. Why count fakes inside the eclipse mask separately?

They show a loss no detector improvement can fix. Mixing them into "missed" would blame the detector for what the mask did.

4. A dip's centre is deeper than (radius ratio)². Why?

Limb darkening: the star's edge is dimmer, so a planet over the bright middle blocks more light than the average.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Vetting
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. Why does a centroid shift during a dip worry us?

It means the dimming light isn't centred on our star. The dip probably comes from a different star in the same big TESS pixel, often a background eclipsing binary.

2. A dip looks perfect but sits 3 hours before a momentum dump. What do we do?

Flag it, don't trust it yet. Check the pixels: spacecraft jitter before dumps faked transits during TOI-1338 b's confirmation. Only if the pixel-level check clears it can it pass C7.

3. What's the circumbinary smoking gun?

Transit durations that change with the binary's phase (shorter near primary eclipse) plus irregular timing that a three-body model predicts. Fakes don't do that.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Pixels and neighbours
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. A neighbour gives 2% of the light and eclipses by 10%. How deep is the dip in our light curve?

0.02 × 0.10 = 0.2% (2,000 ppm): planet-like.

2. Why is a small centroid shift not automatically a problem?

Even a dip on the target moves the centre a little, away from the target (Eq. 11.3). The shift must be compared with what's expected and with the chance spread.

3. Why not just divide the centroid scatter by √N for the error?

That assumes white noise. Pointing drifts are red noise, so the real error is bigger. Measuring the spread of shifts in same-length quiet windows includes it.

4. CROWDSAP is 0.8. A planet's dip in raw SAP data is 800 ppm. What's the true depth?

800 / 0.8 = 1,000 ppm.

docs.title: Chapter 12: STANLEY
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. Why can't a normal planet search stack a two-star planet's crossings?

It assumes the crossings repeat on a fixed timetable with the same length. Two-star planets' crossings shift by hours to days and change length, so a timetable-based stack adds noise instead of signal.

2. Nine crossings, each SNR 2.5 alone. Roughly what SNR does a perfect stack reach?

2.5 × √9 = 7.5: over our bar of 7, though no single crossing is.

3. 28% of orbits scored above 5σ. What does that tell you?

The σ scores aren't "chance" probabilities in this setup. Noise plus thousands of tries makes 5σ common. We need to measure how high noise alone scores before trusting any peak.

4. Why did the peak land at 96.1 days, not 95.2?

The grid only had circular orbits, and the stars' masses in the model differ from the published ones. Both shift the best-fitting period a little.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Our mistakes, as lessons
docs.text:
Read the chapter

1. Three of the number mistakes were caught while writing labs. Why do labs catch mistakes?

A lab must print real output from real data. A wrong assumption in a report can sit unnoticed; in a lab it produces output that doesn't make sense (a period off the grid, a star with no eclipses), and someone has to explain it.

2. Which lesson does the morph = −1 mistake belong to, and what's the general rule?

Lesson 1. Catalogues use codes like −1, 0 or "nan" for "missing". Any cut like "less than 0.5" must decide on purpose what happens to them.

3. Why log mistakes at all? It's embarrassing.

So the next person (or session) doesn't repeat them, so you can judge how much to trust the work, and because a hidden mistake keeps doing damage. A logged one turns into a rule.

docs.title: The story so far
docs.text:
Start here · about 12 min · no maths

In plain words

We're hunting for planets that orbit two stars at once, using free public data from NASA's TESS telescope. So far we've built a search tool, tested it honestly on a planet that's already known, and chosen 549 two-star systems to search. No new planet yet, and we haven't searched the 549 yet. The search is paused while you catch up with this book.

What this page answers: what happened, in order, and where we stand today. Each day has a longer lesson in the Field notes.

docs.title: The idea in one paragraph
docs.text: Some stars come in pairs, two suns orbiting each other. A planet can orbit the pair, like Tatooine. When it passes in front of one of the suns, that sun dims a little: a transit (Chapter 2). With two moving suns, the transits don't arrive on a timetable (Chapter 5), so the usual search methods miss them. That's our opening. NASA's Kepler telescope found thousands of two-star systems between 2009 and 2013 LIKELY. TESS has been watching many of them again since 2018. A planet whose orbit has slowly tilted into view could be crossing now, in TESS data nobody has searched this way. That campaign is called G1.

docs.text:
• 25 rounds of questions set the rules: what we hunt, how sure we must be, what you decide and what I decide. They're in RESEARCH-PLAN.md.
  • Research waves. I read what's known: only 14 transiting two-sun planets exist VERIFIED. I measured how big TESS files are on your PC VERIFIED and checked who else searches.
  • G1 chosen. From your phone you said: "your searches are great. Follow it."
  • This book was founded, with a quiet, professional look (your rule: not gamey).

docs.title: Night 1: 19 to 20 October, the overnight run
docs.text:
1. A better detector. Version 2 of our search re-found the known planet TOI-1338 b in 4 of the 8 sectors where it crossed VERIFIED. It sees planets down to about 6 Earth sizes in one sector VERIFIED. Noise alone still makes fake dips VERIFIED. Chapter 8
  2. A prediction came true. A 2024 paper predicted TOI-1338 b would cross on 16 December 2025. Our search found it that night VERIFIED, about 56 minutes late. That's interesting, but not proof of anything.
  3. Cleaning fakes automatically failed. Rejecting dips near spacecraft events also threw away real ones. So now we flag those dips for a human instead.
  4. The G1 list was frozen: 549 stars from Kepler's catalogue VERIFIED, with fingerprints of the source files.
  5. QLP data was fixed. Half of G1 only has QLP light curves (Chapter 3), and they were full of fake dips from scattered light. The fix borrows NASA's good time windows.
  6. Our first real G1 star, Kepler-16: one dip flagged, and on inspection it was the telescope wobbling before a thruster firing. Nothing survived. Chapter 10
  7. STANLEY (the professionals' search tool, Part 5) was installed and run on TOI-1338. It pointed near the right period, but its scores aren't calibrated yet.

docs.title: Morning 20 October
docs.text:
• Compass was born: your review system that checks every big idea before we build it. Its first verdict on our upgrade plans was REVISE.
  • Realistic fake planets finally worked after I found a bug in STANLEY. Our cleaning keeps 90 to 100% of each dip. We find 6-Earth-size planets 8 times in 10, and about 1 crossing in 11 is lost inside the stars' eclipses VERIFIED.
  • NASA's candidate site now wants papers first VERIFIED. That's a decision for you, later.
  • Afternoon: the Bible Overhaul. Writing the labs caught three of our own errors (a noise number, STANLEY's best period, and a hole in the G1 list), all corrected and logged. The field note has the details.
  • Evening: the quality-filter test (a seventh test in Chapter 8). A milder data filter finds the two crossings we couldn't see before, but costs sensitivity elsewhere; and the raw flux gave a quieter noise estimate than the cleaned flux in several sectors. One star only; nothing in the detector changed. Field note.
  • 21 October: the readiness bar. The home page now shows how complete our plan is (36 of 100), built so that every point needs proof. The hunt is on hold until you say start. Field note.
  • 23 October: the book was rebuilt around a map of the real sky, with three tabs, optional labs and a review page for each Part. Nothing about the science changed. Field note.
